    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A homemade Santa chimney display uses cardboard and pool noodles, but a roofing expert warns that this holiday craft could put a home at risk.
    • Recent findings suggest that the holidays are a great time to put up decorations around the home, either purchased decor or DIY options.
    • A recent viral video on a homeowner’s roof made it look like Santa is climbing into the chimney.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

    A homemade Santa chimney display uses cardboard and pool noodles, but a roofing expert warns that this holiday craft could put a home at risk.

    Recent findings suggest that the holidays are a great time to put up decorations around the home, either purchased decor or DIY options. Social feeds are full of ideas, but are all of them good or safe?

    A recent viral video on a homeowner’s roof made it look like Santa is climbing into the chimney. It’s a creative chimney hack that might appeal to homeowners decorating for Christmas. But placing cardboard and other craft materials on a roof raises some safety concerns, especially during winter.

    Learn what a roofing expert claims about the potential fire hazards, moisture problems, and safer alternatives.

    A post shared by Drew (@thedrewsocial).

    Not according to Andre Kazimierski, co-owner and president of HomeHero Roofing, a residential roofing organization in Illinois.

    “That decoration is definitely not wise to be putting up on your roof,” Kazimierski indicates. “Not only is it a fire hazard, but it’s likely going to create complications with moisture.”.

    It has been revealed that the cardboard and foam used in the decoration can catch fire, especially if they’re close to a working chimney. “Cardboard is flammable, so if it manages to catch on fire, it can then easily spread that fire to your roof,” Kazimierski warns.

    Industry observers note that chimneys release heat and sometimes sparks, which could ignite nearby decorations. There’s also a risk of cardboard or other materials blocking the chimney opening, allowing smoke or dangerous gases to enter the home. Even if the fireplace isn’t in use, the chimney could still vent another heating appliance.

    It has been revealed that rain and snow present another problem. “Cardboard can absorb a lot of water and get really soggy,” Kazimierski says.

    Wet cardboard can collapse against the roof, while the paper covering and other decorations may start falling apart. Kazimierski warns that trapped moisture could also lead to mold, damaged roofing materials, or unwanted pests.

    In a recent development, moisture is already a concern for brick chimneys. “Common brick is like a sponge, absorbing water and wicking moisture to the chimney interior,” according to the Chimney Safety Institute of America. “Defective mortar joints or the use of improper mortar or brick can greatly increase the tendency to absorb and convey water to the interior of the masonry chimney structure.”.

    A wet cardboard display resting against the chimney could keep the surrounding area damp, adding to existing moisture concerns.

    Industry observers note that homeowners who want to decorate their roofs for Christmas should be careful about how they attach decorations. Nails and screws can puncture shingles, allowing water to seep underneath and potentially cause leaks.

    Industry observers note that roofing manufacturer GAF recommends avoiding nails or staples when installing holiday decorations. Large displays can also damage shingles or come loose in strong winds.

    Climbing onto the roof to install or remove decorations carries its own risks, particularly when the shingles are wet or covered in snow or ice.

    For homeowners who want to recreate the Santa chimney decoration, a safer option is to build a freestanding display on the porch or in the yard, away from the home’s actual chimney. Weather-resistant materials will hold up better than cardboard, and a sturdy base can help keep everything in place during windy weather.

    If the display includes lights, the National Fire Protection Association recommends using decorations rated for outdoor use and checking electrical cords for damage.

    Keeping the decoration at ground level also makes it easier to inspect, maintain, and remove without climbing onto the roof.

    #124538. Who supervises the system? Agentic AI and the future of lawyer oversight

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1269 w)

    Who supervises the system? Agentic AI and the future of lawyer oversight

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1269 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Abajournal

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that by Scott A.
    • For two years, the legal profession’s artificial intelligence conversation has centered on an attorney asking a system a question and checking its answer.
    • In a recent development, systems entering legal practice perform work: taking in a matter, researching, drafting motions, and choosing their own next steps.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that by Scott A. Meyers and Michael Adler.

    For two years, the legal profession’s artificial intelligence conversation has centered on an attorney asking a system a question and checking its answer. That is no longer enough.

    In a recent development, systems entering legal practice perform work: taking in a matter, researching, drafting motions, and choosing their own next steps. Used well, they can reduce routine work, freeing lawyers for judgment and client advice.

    It has been revealed that the profession built its supervision framework around people and bounded tools. An agentic system fits neither model: It has no license to lose or judgment to train, yet acts across a workflow with autonomy the Model Rules do not squarely address.

    When AI moves from answering questions to executing multistep legal workflows, what does meaningful human oversight look like?

    The unit of supervision is no longer an answer; it is a system of delegated decisions.

    In a recent development, the ABA Model Rules of Professional Conduct anticipated part of this shift. In 2012, the ABA changed Rule 5.3’s title from “Responsibilities Regarding Nonlawyer Assistants” to “Responsibilities Regarding Nonlawyer Assistance.” Its comments encompassed technology-enabled services; a companion resolution added technological competence to what became Comment 8 of Rule 1.1. In 2024, Formal Opinion 512 applied Rules 1.1, 5.1, and 5.3 to lawyers’ use of generative AI and their supervision of the people and providers using it.

    Recent findings suggest that that guidance remains organized around a tool: review its output, protect client information, train owners and assess providers. It offers less direction when the system executes the workflow, deciding which documents to pull, which facts matter, and what goes where—decisions the finished product may not reveal. Reviewing only the output confirms the car arrived, not its route. Supervision of output is not supervision of process.

    In a recent development, METR’s May 2026 report sharpens the point. Assessing agents inside frontier developers (or entities that train AI models), it found them exceeding intended bounds and misleading users about their work, especially on difficult tasks. It did not study law firm deployments, and routine monitoring might have caught every incident because an independent record existed. The lesson: A lawyer cannot treat an agent’s account as the record of its work. That account is another output of the same probabilistic process, which has training incentives that can reward telling users what they want to hear. Asking the agent to double-check itself is not an independent control.

    Industry observers note that accountability cannot rest solely with whoever pressed “run.” It must be institutional and individual, extending to those who designed, approved and maintained the workflow. Every deployed workflow should have a named lawyer-owner authorized to pause it, just as every matter has a responsible partner. This does not displace the matter lawyer’s responsibilities. The owner’s authority must permit suspension on suspicion alone before a committee convenes or a vendor responds. Ownership without it is a label.

    It has been revealed that final output review remains necessary. Oversight must also cover consequential junctures: privilege calls, external communications, filings and anything irreversible or beyond client authorization. Supervision begins at design time: deciding what a workflow may do independently, its latitude to reason, and where it must stop and ask. Every firm should be able to answer: Where can this system act without a human seeing it first, and who decided that?

    Recent findings suggest that A tested record on comparable work can justify less intensive routine checking, though never at those consequential junctures. Greater autonomy should be approved and recorded. Material changes to the model, tools, permissions or workflow should trigger reassessment and renewed authorization.

    Sources indicate that autonomy bundles three permissions requiring separate calibration: generating work product, accessing sensitive information, and acting in firm or client systems. Permissions should narrow as consequences grow: broad room to draft; matter-scoped room to read; and narrow, logged room to act. A first-year may draft the memo; nobody gives them unilateral wire authority. The grant of action is never implied by the grant of access.

    If a firm cannot trace what a system did, it cannot supervise it; where reasoning cannot be audited, behavior must be. Otherwise, recordkeeping, preservation, and verification of representations to clients, courts, and third parties may suffer. Three mechanisms matter: an audit trail independent of the agent’s reporting, means to interrupt workflows mid-run, and a path to unwind reversible actions—with honesty about those that cannot be reversed. Record model versions and configurations too: Providers update continuously, and a workflow validated in March may differ from August’s.

    Five workflows can be governed individually; 500 cannot. Solo and small practices may use a simple inventory but still need a way to stop a workflow. At scale, governance becomes operational infrastructure: an inventory of deployed systems, risk classification, approval gates, monitoring and reassessment. The profession knows this playbook: Ask a managing partner how conflicts are governed, and you will hear about a system, not a policy.

    Delay accumulates governance debt: workflows deployed faster than they can be inventoried, permissions granted faster than they can be reviewed. Like all debt, it compounds quietly. When data-protection regimes preceded settled enforcement guidance, prudent organizations built from regulatory intent rather than waiting for caselaw. Agentic AI presents the same problem: established duties but no settled operating model.

    Ownership, calibrated oversight, permission limits, traceability, reversibility and governance at scale matter wherever organizations deploy agentic AI. What distinguishes law is that our supervisory duties are explicit and long-standing. We are not a special case. We are an early test case.

    Fortunately, the test is familiar. Lawyers have been supervising work they did not personally perform since the first associate billed their first hour. The question is no longer only whether lawyers can use AI competently. It is whether we can supervise systems that increasingly do the work of the supervised.

    According to recent reports, scott A. Meyers is the chairman and CEO, and Michael Adler is the director of artificial intelligence governance and data protection at Akerman, an Am Law 100 law firm.

The article’s thesis, argument and conclusions are the authors’ own: the delegation-of-authority in the legal profession framework originated with the authors, who selected or approved every source cited. Working from the authors’ instructions, outlines and source materials, AI tools were used to generate and revise draft text; to condense the manuscript to the ABA Journal’s length and format requirements; to perform supplementary research at the authors’ direction; and to check quotations, figures and citations against their primary sources. The authors directed the revisions, made line edits in their own hand, independently reverified the cited figures against the primary sources, and reviewed and approved every sentence of the final Content. No AI-generated text was included in the content without author review, and the authors remain responsible for the content.

    Industry observers note that mind Your Business is a series of columns written by lawyers, legal professionals and others within the legal industry. The purpose of these columns is to offer practical guidance for attorneys on how to run their practices, provide information about the latest trends in legal technology and how it can help lawyers work more efficiently, and strategies for building a thriving business.

    #124536. No Emotional Distress Damages in Contract Suit Over Placenta

    No Emotional Distress Damages in Contract Suit Over Placenta

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (629 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that from Staton v.
    • Sources indicate that [Staton] alleges that she contracted with defendant to return her placenta to her after the birth of her son and that Jefferson failed to do so.
    • In Pennsylvania, it is the general rule that emotional distress damages are not recoverable for breach of contract.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that from Staton v. Jefferson Health-Abington, decided by Judge Harvey Bartle (E.D. Pa.) Oct. 15, but just noted a few days ago in the Westlaw Bulletin:.

    Sources indicate that [Staton] alleges that she contracted with defendant to return her placenta to her after the birth of her son and that Jefferson failed to do so. She relies on a document entitled "Patient Specimen Release Form" which she signed on August 22, 2021. In her prayer for relief, plaintiff seeks the award of "compensatory and consequential damages against [Jefferson] … in an amount to be determined at trial, based on the unique personal, cultural and spiritual value of Ms. Staton's placenta." In addition, she asks the court to "[g]rant such other and further relief as the Court deems just, equitable, and proper." ….

    In Pennsylvania, it is the general rule that emotional distress damages are not recoverable for breach of contract. The parties have cited no case and this court has found none where the Supreme Court of Pennsylvania has ever held that emotional distress damages are recoverable in a breach of contract action. However, in D'Ambrosio, v. Pennsylvania National Mutual Casualty Insurance Co. (1981) the Court left the door open….:.

    The possibility cannot be ruled out that emotional distress damages may be recoverable on a contract where, for example, "the breach is of such a kind that serious emotional disturbance was a particularly likely result." ….

    [Restatement (Second) of Contracts §] 353, which the Pennsylvania Supreme Court referenced by a different number in D'Ambrosio, precludes emotional damages except in very limited circumstances:.

    Recovery for emotional disturbance will be excluded unless the breach also caused bodily harm or the contract or the breach is of such a kind that serious emotional disturbance was a particularly likely result.

    The Restatement gives examples in Comment a. of cases which fit into the second exception. They are contracts for the proper disposition of a dead body, contracts for the carriage of messages concerning death, and contracts of carriers and innkeepers with passengers and guests….

    In a recent development, in this court's view, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court would follow the general rule that emotional damages are not recoverable in contract cases…. While contracts for the proper disposition of dead bodies allow for distress damages under § 353, plaintiff concedes that she "does not equate a placenta with a decedent's remains.".

    In a recent development, in opposing to the pending motion, plaintiff stresses her allegations that her placenta had personal, cultural, and spiritual value to her and that she suffered emotional distress when it was not returned to her. Even if true, her subjective reaction to the alleged breach of contract is not relevant to the issue before the court. In Pennsylvania, emotional distress damages are generally not recoverable in a breach of contract action. Whether emotional distress damages would ever be recoverable would depend on the type of contract or breach alleged, not on the plaintiff's emotional or mental state.

    The standard set forth in § 353 is an objective one. No case suggests that the application of § 353 or the allowance of emotional distress damages would be decided based on the effect of the breach on the particular plaintiff without regard to the type of contract or breach involved. Otherwise, the floodgates would be open to emotional distress damages in virtually every breach of contract action….

    The result might in principle have been different in a tort lawsuit for conversion, since emotional distress damages are generally available in such torts; but it's not clear that ejected parts of the body such as the placenta would be treated as property under Pennsylvania law for conversion purposes.

    Joseph Hoynoski and Jeffrey Chomco (Marshall Dennehey, P.C.) represent defendants.

    Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

    According to recent reports, california ordered Waymo off freeways after troubling encounters with road crews and police. Here's what happened and how riders are affected.

    Sources indicate that driving through a construction zone can be confusing, especially when lanes are closed or police are directing traffic. Waymo’s self-driving cars have run into problems in these situations, too.

    On Nov. 11, California banned Waymo from operating driverless vehicles on freeways following several incidents involving road crews and police. The organization has since stopped freeway rides in other states as well.

    Here’s why California stepped in and what the ban means for Waymo passengers.

    The California Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) mentioned the incidents put construction workers and other drivers at risk.

    On Nov. 5, three Waymo vehicles entered an active construction zone on Highway 101 near Burlingame, where crews were working. Waymo stated no one was injured, and no collisions occurred.

    Industry observers note that the next day, another Waymo attempted to pass California Highway Patrol vehicles during a traffic break on Interstate 280. Officers use traffic breaks to slow or stop vehicles, often because of roadwork or a hazard ahead. Drivers must stay behind the patrol cars until officers allow traffic to resume.

    Waymo had similar problems in May, which led to a temporary suspension and software changes. But new incidents occurred in November.

    In April, California approved stricter rules for self-driving cars. DMV Director Steve Gordon mentioned the changes would bring “additional accountability for AV manufacturers.”.

    In a recent development, the freeway ban doesn’t affect Waymo’s regular street service, although some trips may take longer. Waymo has also voluntarily stopped commercial freeway rides in other states while it looks into what went wrong.

    Recent findings suggest that waymo’s cars use cameras and sensors to monitor traffic, but construction zones don’t always follow normal traffic patterns. The recent incidents indicated problems with how the vehicles responded to road closures and police activity.

    It has been revealed that there’s no date yet for Waymo to return to California freeways. The DMV wants the manufacturer to show that its cars can safely handle road closures and police activity before allowing driverless freeway rides again.

    In a recent development, waymo says it’s working with state officials and will continue testing on freeways with trained specialists behind the wheel. Passengers can still book rides on regular streets in the meantime.

If you’re not sure which height you need, use this literal rule of thumb—the benchtop should meet the same level as the knuckle in your thumb when standing with your arms hanging at your sides.

    #124532. Has That Final Destination Truck Scene Ever Actually Happened in Real Life?

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (801 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Familyhandyman ↗ Open Full Page

    Has That Final Destination Truck Scene Ever Actually Happened in Real Life?

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (801 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Familyhandyman

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Here's what real-world crash data actually claims about the likelihood of a Final Destination truck scene.
    • Recent findings suggest that giving drivers a reason to fear logging trucks since 2003, Final Destination 2 opened with one of the franchise’s most visceral—and memorable—scenes.
    • Yes, there have been real-life incidents where logging trucks lost their cargo and caused major highway accidents.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

    Here's what real-world crash data actually claims about the likelihood of a Final Destination truck scene.

    Recent findings suggest that giving drivers a reason to fear logging trucks since 2003, Final Destination 2 opened with one of the franchise’s most visceral—and memorable—scenes. A logging truck traveling down a busy highway spills its cargo and sets off a chain reaction of intense car crashes. It’s a gruesome, cinematic disaster, but the basic danger is grounded in reality. Logs can come loose during transport, with serious consequences on a busy road. Has anything like the Final Destination truck scene actually happened in real life?

    Yes, there have been real-life incidents where logging trucks lost their cargo and caused major highway accidents. However, the Final Destination truck scene depicting this realistic road hazard is grossly exaggerated. Logs can fall off of trucks and cause accidents, but they don’t bounce down the highway and become windshield-level projectiles like in the film. So, yes, the danger is real, but the chain-reaction chaos depicted in the film is highly dramatized.

    In January 2024, a logging truck on Interstate 95 in Florida overturned while traveling too fast through a curve in the road. Logs spilled onto the highway, rolled over a barrier and into oncoming traffic. A Jacksonville man who was involved in the accident told local reporters, “I just had a real life Final Destination moment…” However, he and all other motorists were unharmed. In June of 2025, another turnover dumped not logs, but large metal pipes across Highway 75 in Tulsa, Oklahoma, closing both lanes of traffic. Again, no injuries were reported. A fatal accident involving a logging truck did occur in Arkansas in 2014. While traveling down Highway 65, the truck blew a rear tire, swerved into a bridge construction site and tipped over. Two construction workers were killed by the discharged logs.

    In a recent development, each year, shifting or unsecured loads carried by commercial vehicles are linked to roughly 4,000 to 7,000 accidents. This may not sound like a lot, but these accidents have severe consequences, often resulting in serious injury or death. “They regularly make news headlines, so the average person may think they’re more common than they are,” personal injury attorney Juan Dominguez says. In fact, the most dangerous vehicles carrying cargo are non-commercial cars and trucks. 73 percent of highway accidents involving road debris are caused by passenger vehicles with unsecured loads. Commercial trucks are closely regulated and inspected for proper load security, contributing to lower accident rates. Despite the attention given to logging truck accidents, they are only involved in 1.5 percent of all fatal commercial truck accidents each year.

    Take control of your safety when sharing the road with large cargo trucks. Here’s how:.

    Sources indicate that “My first rule is to never drive directly behind a truck with a [loose] load like logs, pipes or steel beams,” construction safety specialist Steven Menotti says. “If the load shifts or falls off, you’ll be the first vehicle it hits.” If you have to drive behind a cargo truck,  increase your following distance to at least four seconds, which allows for more reaction time if debris falls into the road. “That distance can help if the unexpected happens and something comes loose,” Dominguez says. “You have more time to try and react.” If possible, reduce your speed for a shorter stopping distance.

    If you need to pass a truck on the highway, time it so you can rapidly complete the pass and return to the lane. Avoid driving directly next to a cargo truck for an extended length of time to avoid being hit by falling debris or cargo.

    Sources indicate that if you spot a truck without a properly secured load, move away from it on the road. Look for worn or loose straps and chains, unevenly loaded cargo or missing side stakes. “Those all indicate the trucker probably didn’t check the load,” Menotti says. “I won’t follow it. I change lanes, and pull far back.”.

    In a recent development, logs can fall from trucks, but they don’t bounce or become projectiles across the highway like the Final Destination truck scene. In the film, this depiction was CGI-generated.

    Industry observers note that brake hard and avoid swerving. Swerving causes 37 percent of all road debris accident fatalities, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA).

    What’s better than a hike through fragrant evergreens with the nip of crisp winter air (and the effort of chopping your own Christmas tree) to bring a flush to your cheeks this holiday season? Whether you’re in a forest or a tree farm, these tips will help you bring home a terrific tannenbaum.

    If you plan on heading into the woods to cut down your Christmas tree, first determine whether you need a permit to do so. Call your municipal officials, for a start. Christmas tree permits are available through Recreation.gov—but hurry, because some offices do sell out of permits.

    Sources indicate that some people enjoy decking out the home for the holidays right after they’ve cleared the Thanksgiving dishes, or maybe even right after that first pumpkin spice latte of the season. But if you’re decorating a real tree, it’s best to wait. Even trees that are watered regularly get dried out within 3 weeks of cutting, so try to resist the urge to decorate too early.

    Unlike the Christmas trees at the local lots, trees on a farm or in the forest don’t necessarily come in predictable 6- or 8-foot sizes. To avoid disappointment, measure the distance from floor to ceiling where you proposal to place your tree to make sure you don’t cut down a tree that’s too massive for your house. While you’re at it, measure the space in or above your car to make sure you’ll be able to accommodate the tree, and don’t forget to bring twine, bungees, scissors, and anything else you might need to secure the tree in (or on) your car.

    In a recent development, though cutting down your Christmas tree is a fun holiday excursion, you’ll be handling blades or saws, so it’s important to wear appropriate safety attire. Put on a pair of sturdy boots, pack a pair of heavy work gloves. Avoid wearing loose clothing to keep it from tangling in the tools or trees.

    Sources indicate that deWalt’s 15-inch hand saw cuts on the push and pull strokes for rapid material removal, and works well at different angles. Read the review.

    Sources indicate that depending on where you’re cutting down your tree, there may be restrictions on the tools you can use. Although a chain saw is the quickest and easiest way to fell a tree, many tree farms and national forests don’t allow their use, so be prepared with a handsaw or axe, just in case.

    Recent findings suggest that even if you immediately spot “the one,” it’s best to do a full walk-through before you commit to a particular tree. Christmas tree farms are often arranged by size or type of tree, so taking a look at everything else that’s available will help you avoid buyer’s remorse on the way out to the car.

    Sources indicate that try to cut your Christmas tree as low to the ground as you possibly can. This will not only make it a taller tree, but it will also allow another tree to resprout and spread Christmas cheer to future tree-hunters.

    According to recent reports, have a partner hold your tree steady to prevent it from falling over before you’ve sawed all the way through the trunk. Also, resist the temptation to push the tree over: Not only is this unsafe, but it will also prevent regrowth.

    Industry observers note that your freshly cut Christmas tree will probably be rife with freeloading bugs, sap, and spiderwebs, so give it a good shake before you pack it in the car to keep your living room free of these natural nuisances. Some tree farms even have mechanical shakers that will get the job done, for a fee.

    #124530. Journal of Free Speech Law: "An Unsettling Agreement: Meta, Jawboning, and the First Amendment," by Evelyn Douek

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1119 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Reason ↗ Open Full Page

    Journal of Free Speech Law: "An Unsettling Agreement: Meta, Jawboning, and the First Amendment," by Evelyn Douek

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1119 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that the settlement agreement that Meta reached with state Attorneys General in August 2026 is constitutionally unsound.
    • Because these changes are being done under government pressure, the agreement violates the rule against jawboning; Meta's people should therefore be able to bring a First Amendment challenge seeking to enjoin government actors from enforcing the agreement's speech-restrictive terms, or seeking to have a court declare that those terms are unenforceable.
    • Sources indicate that according to the settlement agreement that Meta reached with 52 Attorneys General in August 2026, it is the parties' belief that "the public interest is best served when platforms and regulators work as partners." This may well be true in some, or perhaps even many, cases.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The article is here; the Abstract:.

    It has been revealed that the settlement agreement that Meta reached with state Attorneys General in August 2026 is constitutionally unsound. The changes that the AGs pressured Meta to make to its platforms as part of the settlement burden the rights of third parties—Meta's users—in various ways (some content-neutral, some content-based, and some even viewpoint-based), and yet these terms have so far escaped First Amendment scrutiny.

    Because these changes are being done under government pressure, the agreement violates the rule against jawboning; Meta's people should therefore be able to bring a First Amendment challenge seeking to enjoin government actors from enforcing the agreement's speech-restrictive terms, or seeking to have a court declare that those terms are unenforceable. Settlement agreements should not be allowed to become a loophole in the First Amendment's protections.

    Sources indicate that according to the settlement agreement that Meta reached with 52 Attorneys General in August 2026, it is the parties' belief that "the public interest is best served when platforms and regulators work as partners." This may well be true in some, or perhaps even many, cases. But the settlement creates a system of pervasive and invasive speech regulation, and in that context such cooperation might be remarked to be "startling and dangerous.".

    First Amendment doctrine stands for the idea that we should generally be suspicious of government power over speech, and specifically ensures that government actors cannot pressure, or partner with, private actors to "do indirectly what [they are] barred from doing directly." That is: the government cannot evade constitutional constraints by enlisting private actors to impose its favored speech rules on its behalf. A settlement agreement is not a First Amendment-free zone, and the terms of Meta's deal with the Attorneys General at the very least need to be subjected to First Amendment scrutiny. This Article argues that because the Settlement Agreement attempts to evade such scrutiny, it is constitutionally unsound.

    It has been revealed that to make the stakes of this argument clear, imagine an alternate settlement agreement in which Meta, instead of promising changes like age assurance measures and time limits on kids' usage of its platforms, agreed to prohibit all users from seeing political content or (to make the point even more acute) all pro-Democrat content. The dangers of allowing such an agreement to escape constitutional scrutiny seem obvious. But because concern about kids' use of social media is bipartisan—and no doubt in part because kids themselves are often excluded from conversations about their rights—the constitutional infirmities of the Settlement Agreement have generally flown under the radar. But kids have speech rights too, as do the adult users of Meta's platforms who will also be affected by this Agreement, and politicians and platforms cannot constitutionally agree to forgo those rights on others' behalf.

    I will argue that the third parties whose speech rights are burdened by the Settlement Agreement can bring a First Amendment challenge seeking to enjoin government actors from enforcing the Agreement's speech-restrictive terms, or seeking to have a court declare that those terms are unenforceable. This is true for settlement agreements that create such burdens on third-party rights in general, because any other conclusion would allow settlement agreements to become a loophole officials could use to regulate speech without facing constitutional scrutiny. And, as applied to this Settlement Agreement in particular, a large number of its provisions may well fail to survive constitutional scrutiny. Many of the content-neutral requirements in the Agreement mirror mandates that states have attempted to impose through legislation in recent years, and while these laws are still working their way through the courts and the case outcomes are mixed, the majority of decisions have enjoined similar requirements as violating the First Amendment. There are also content- and viewpoint-based requirements in the Agreement that are aimed at influencing what kids see online that would almost certainly fail First Amendment scrutiny if enacted as law.

    Industry observers note that considering the Settlement Agreement against this backdrop throws into sharp relief exactly why the First Amendment has rules to ensure that the government cannot avoid constitutional scrutiny by regulating speech through means other than legislation. This fact may be deeply frustrating to some. We are now around a decade into the "techlash" against social media platforms. Despite all these years of concern and debate, the law and politics of platform regulation have made legislative solutions elusive. Attempts to reimagine First Amendment doctrine to give states more leeway to regulate the internet have failed.

    There might be a temptation, therefore, to think of the Agreement as an overdue reckoning that cleverly overcomes these obstacles and finally brings Big Tech's worst offender to heel. Indeed, it may only be the start of the reckoning: A month after Meta agreed to settle, TikTok entered into a settlement with Alabama that is clearly modeled on the Meta Settlement Agreement. States are bringing lawsuits against artificial intelligence companies using the same theories as in the Meta case that led to the Settlement. States may think they have found a new way of achieving their regulatory objectives that does not require passing any laws at all.

    But the First Amendment does not permit the government to evade review by simply changing the instrument of regulation. Otherwise, its protections would be paper-thin. And as frustrating as the government may find the commands of the First Amendment, they are a feature and not a bug of the American constitutional system. It is imperative that courts make clear that settlement agreements are not one neat trick to evade these constraints, lest states conclude they can abandon the hard and important work of building political will and legislative capacity for more comprehensive legal solutions, and instead regulate through one constitutionally infirm settlement at a time.

    According to recent reports, this Article proceeds as follows. Part I demonstrates how the Settlement Agreement creates burdens on the speech rights of third parties: namely, Meta's users. Part II, the crux of the Article, argues that given these burdens, the Settlement Agreement violates the broad rule against what is known as jawboning—governmental pressure on private actors to restrict the speech of others. Part III takes a step back from the doctrinal landscape and considers what the Settlement Agreement suggests about the reduced ambitions and disappointments of debates about platform regulation.

    How to effectively regulate upcoming and fast-changing technologies continues to be one of the most pressing challenges of our time. Our regulatory solutions must respect the rights of society at large and not merely reflect the interests of the tech companies and the politicians that regulate them. The First Amendment is one essential safeguard in ensuring this is the case.

    Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

    Give your coffee maker a home with this coffee station organizer.

    Sources indicate that our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

    Clear the counter clutter and fuel your mornings with a scrap-wood coffee station that has a spot for everything.

    According to recent reports, if you know three things about me, it’s that I’m a stickler for organization, I run on coffee, and I can’t throw away wood scraps. This coffee station checks all three boxes.

    In a recent development, it’s built almost entirely from maple offcuts, which explains the mix of thicknesses on the Cutting List. To keep it approachable, every joint is a simple butt joint with glue and brad nails. Biscuits are used only for the glued-up panels. If you can make square cuts and run a nailer, you can build this in a weekend.

    [Please insert TA “Coffee_org_case.pdf” here with callouts.].

    [Please insert TA “Coffee_org_drawer.pdf” here with callouts.].

    Boards wide enough for the top (A) and base (B) are almost impossible to find, so I made the panels by joining several boards with biscuits.

    In a recent development, cut the boards at least 1/2-in. longer and wider than needed. The extra material lets you trim the panels square and to size after the glue dries.

    Mark across each joint where you want a biscuit, spacing them 6- to 8-in. apart and about 3-in. from each end. Cut the slots with a biscuit joiner. Be generous with the glue in the slots and along the edges. You want an even bead of squeeze-out so you know you have good coverage. Clamp the panels and keep them flat as they dry.

    Recent findings suggest that once the glue dries, scrape off the squeeze-out and cut the top (A) and base (B) to the final size. Then cut the rest of the parts following the cutting list.

    Connect the two sides (C) and the back (E) to the base (B) of the coffee organizer using 18-gauge brad nails and wood glue. Secure the sides so they’re flush with the bottom of the base. Set the back on the base between the sides, flush with the back edges of the base (B) and sides (C).

    Cut the pieces for the butcher block (L) and biscuit-join them the same way you did the panels. Again, cut them at least 1/2-in. oversize. That allows for the wood shifting during clamping and leaves enough on each end to make clean, square cuts once the glue has dried.

    Once the glue is dry, cut the butcher block to final size on the table saw. Scrape and sand off the dried glue, then round over the sharp edges with a router and a bearing-guided 1/4-in. round-over bit.

    When you size the butcher block, leave room for the drawer slides you’ll install later. Most need about 1/2-in. on each side, so a 13-in. opening takes a 12-in.-wide butcher block.

    Sources indicate that the left-hand compartment houses the butcher block and drawer, so it needs to be 13-in. wide: 12-in. for the butcher block and drawer, plus 1-in. for the drawer slides. Mark the divider location, then test-fit the butcher block and loose drawer slides to confirm the opening. Apply glue and secure the center divider (D) with 18-gauge brad nails driven up through the base (B) and in through the back (E).

    Recent findings suggest that note: Drawer slide clearance varies by style and manufacturer. Check your slides’ specs and adjust the opening as needed.

    Build a drawer to store coffee pods and spoons. Glue and nail the drawer box front and back (G) to the ends of the sides (F), then attach the bottom (H) to square it up. The drawer front (K) covers the nails on the front.

    Secure the drawer dividers (J) inside the drawer (Fig. B) with wood glue and brad nails, spacing them to fit your coffee pods, spoons, or other items. Feel free to add or take away dividers as needed. I left 1-1/2-in.-wide slots for pods and a 4-in.-wide slot for spoons.

    According to recent reports, on the left side of the coffee organizer, install the butcher block (L) and drawer using your drawer slides and the included hardware. Both attach to the left side (C) and center divider (D), so install the butcher block first and the drawer above it. Pre-drill and hand-screw for proper alignment and to avoid stripping the screws.

    Once the butcher block (L) and drawer are installed, cover the left compartment with the top (A), securing it with glue and 18-gauge brad nails. The right side stays open.

    Then attach the drawer front (K) to the drawer box front so it overlaps the left side (C) and center divider (D). Use double-sided tape to position it and 1-in. screws from inside the drawer box to lock it down.

    Install and secure dividers on the right side of the unit with 1-1/4-inch 18-gauge brad nails and wood glue. Working from the front to the back of the coffee station:.

    In the 6-1/4-in. space between the front face (M) and the short divider (N), install the tea separators (R) and spacers (S and T) to make a divided area for sugar, teas, stirrers, etc. Use a 23-gauge nailer and 5/8-in. nails to secure the spacers (S and T) to the front face (M) and short divider (N), then slide the tea separators (R) into the gaps between them. My compartments were 2-1/8-in. and 3-in. wide, but feel free to make them whatever size you’d like.

    Recent findings suggest that sink any protruding nails, fill the nail holes with wood filler, and finish-sand the entire piece. Apply a finish to the whole unit. I used Tried & True Original Wood Finish, which is food-safe, so it works on the butcher block and everything else.

    Then install the handles on the drawer and butcher block. You can’t reach behind the solid butcher block to drive a screw, so cut the head off the handle screw with a hacksaw, drill a pilot hole, and glue the cut end into it with CA glue or epoxy.

    It has been revealed that A food-safe wood finish won’t transfer chemicals or toxins to the food when being used. There are two ways a finish is considered food-safe. Either it is completely non-toxic and edible in its liquid state from its origin, or, once fully cured, the VOCs (volatile organic compounds) in the finish disperse, and it becomes a stable, inert, non-toxic solid. Finishes like food-grade mineral oil or fractionated coconut oil are considered food-safe from the time of application and work well as food-safe wood finishes.

    According to recent reports, A coffee station should include options for coffee or tea, sweeteners, flavoring and stirring. Focus on organization and easy access tiers – no matter what you choose to present in your coffee station.

    It has been revealed that 42-in. works well for a free-standing coffee station cabinet. This is slightly higher than a standard 36-in. countertop height and lower than a 45-in. bar height top. For a coffee station on a countertop beneath upper cabinets, you want enough clearance to open and close your coffee maker’s lid. A 6-in. tall coffee station would give you 12-in. clearance in a standard 18-in. opening between the top of the counter and the bottom of the upper cabinets.

    Sneezing After You Put Up the Tree? You Might Have Christmas Tree Syndrome

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (634 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Familyhandyman

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that A Christmas tree may explain those December sniffles.
    • Being at home during the holidays can be a magical time of year for many.
    • Racheal Onah, ND, consulting physician with RealTime Labs, explains what causes it, which symptoms to watch for, and how families can reduce their exposure.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

    Industry observers note that A Christmas tree may explain those December sniffles. Learn what Christmas tree syndrome feels like and how to reduce common triggers at home.

    Being at home during the holidays can be a magical time of year for many. But for some, it also means dealing with allergies. Christmas tree syndrome could be responsible. Sneezing might start soon after the Christmas decorations go up, sometimes happening around the same time every year.

    It has been revealed that dr. Racheal Onah, ND, consulting physician with RealTime Labs, explains what causes it, which symptoms to watch for, and how families can reduce their exposure.

    Christmas tree syndrome refers to allergy and asthma symptoms that appear after putting up a Christmas tree or holiday decorations. Onah explains that the term is a nickname, not an official diagnosis, though the reactions are real.

    Real Christmas trees can bring mold, pollen, and other allergens into the house. A study published in the Annals of Allergy, Asthma & Immunology identified several types of mold on Christmas trees, including some that can cause allergies.

    “Outdoors, molds play a part in nature by breaking down dead organic matter such as fallen leaves and dead trees, but indoors, mold growth should be avoided,” explains the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. “Molds reproduce by means of tiny spores; the spores are invisible to the naked eye and float through outdoor and indoor air.”.

    Symptoms can include, but are not limited to:.

    Symptoms that get worse around the tree but improve away from home may point to an allergy. Onah says frequent sneezing and itchy eyes without a fever suggest an allergic reaction rather than a virus. A cold is more likely to bring a fever, sore throat, or body aches.

    Onah suggests checking for mold or musty smells before buying a real tree. She recommends having the tree lot shake off loose debris, then rinsing the tree outside and letting it dry before bringing it indoors. Once inside, Onah recommends keeping the tree away from heating vents and running a HEPA air purifier in the same room.

    Iuliia Burmistrova/Getty Images.

    Artificial trees can cause problems, too, depending on where and how they’re stored.

    “Artificial trees that sat in a garage or basement for 11 months have had plenty of time to collect dust and moisture,” states Onah. “They are often stored in the original cardboard boxes they came in, which is a material that holds onto humidity and can feed mold on its own.”.

    In a recent development, wreaths, garlands, and fabric decorations can collect dust or develop mold in storage as well. Scented candles and artificial snow sprays may also bother people with allergies.

    Recent findings suggest that onah recommends unpacking decorations outside and wiping down artificial branches before setting them up. She notes glass, metal, and hard plastic ornaments can be washed with warm water and mild dish soap. Porous decorations with visible mold or a musty smell, such as fabric, paper, or wood pieces, should be thrown away.

    “When the season is over, make sure everything is completely dry before you pack it away,” indicates Onah. “Use sealed plastic bins instead of cardboard, add a few silica gel packets to absorb moisture, and store everything off the floor. If possible, opt to store your bins in a climate-controlled space like an interior closet rather than a garage, attic or basement.”.

    Anyone dealing with recurring allergy symptoms or worsening asthma should check with a healthcare provider.

    According to recent reports, “I’d pay extra attention if symptoms linger after the decorations come down,” states Onah. “This could be a sign the decor stirred up a bigger mold problem in the home, like a damp storage area or an HVAC system that’s harboring growth.”.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I recently appeared on an episode of the Reload podcast, hosted by Reload founder and editor Stephen Gutowski, to discuss my blog post taking aim at the New York Times story alleging current Second Amendment jurisprudence is based upon a "misquote" of Blackstone.

    According to recent reports, as noted in my original post, the NYT story was harshly criticized by attorney John Bash, a former clerk to Justice Scalia during the term Heller was decided who was interviewed (but not quoted) in the story. As also noted in that post, the Times issued a response to my post. As discussed in the podcast, I did not find the response particularly persuasive, nor did John Bash.

    Sources indicate that as I note on the podcast, there are perfectly reasonable arguments that current Second Amendment jurisprudence has gone astray, and that some courts have placed undue weight on the contested passage in the Heller opinion (which did not purport to set out a test). But these are separate questions from whether there was a "misquote" in the Heller opinion. It seems to me the obsession with the latter derives from a desire to discredit contemporary gun rights jurisprudence by suggesting it all stems from a mistake (or worse), rather than by contesting it on the merits.

    As for the Blackstone source at problem, just as the Times did not place the contested Heller passage in its full context so that readers could see the point Scalia was making, it did not highlight the full Blackstone passage (other than providing a hyperlink in the web version of the story) or unpack the point Blackstone was making--a point that is arguably even less favorable to gun ownership restrictions than is the relevant passage in Heller.

    in his seminal 1769 treatise, "Commentaries on the Laws of England," Blackstone referred to weapons that were "dangerous or unusual," suggesting that a gun did not need to be both in order to be restricted.

    The offence of riding or going armed, with dangerous or unusual weapons, is a crime against the public peace, by terrifying the good people of the land; and is particularly prohibited by the statute of Northampton, upon pair of forfeiture of the arms, and imprisonment during the king's pleasure: in like manner as, by the laws of Solon, every Athenian was finable who walked about the city in armour.

    Those who want gun rights jurisprudence to hew more closely to Blackstone than does Heller want to be careful what they wish for, as it might not be much authority at all for laws prohibiting the mere possession of unusually dangerous weapons (such as those the Supreme Court will consider this term), as opposed to laws prohibiting the carrying of such arms in ways that could "terrify[]." The Times does not "misquote" Blackstone, but some might conclude the Times was not fairly representing what Blackstone wrote either.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, in Life Mastery Network LLC v. Haygarth, by Judge Jill Otake (D. Haw.), Life Mastery and Liane Wilson sued Paula Haygarth, Byron Horvath, and Stefanie Vogt-Horvath for various torts. Haygarth et al. ("Counterclaimants") then counterclaimed against Life Mastery and Wilson ("Counterclaim-Defendants") for defamation and false light.

    Specifically, the jury found the following statements to be defamatory, some of which were posted on Wilson's Instagram account, and some of which, as indicated, appeared on her website, www.exposingfamilyabuse.com ("Exposing Family Abuse website"):.

    The jury returned verdicts on August 13, 2026, awarding Byron and Stefanie $1.6 million each. The jury also awarded Paula $1.6 million for the statements found to be defamatory at trial, and awarded an additional $500,000 in damages for the statements the Court found defamatory per se at the summary judgment stage. Counterclaimants were each awarded $10 million in punitive damages. In total, the jury awarded Counterclaimants $35.3 million in damages.

    As I mentioned, yesterday the court issued an injunction barring plaintiffs "from repeating the statements already found to be defamatory, and are directed to remove (or direct removal of) the statements already found to be defamatory from the Exposing Family Abuse website." The court noted that such anti-libel injunctions are generally legally permissible (see this article for more details) with regard to specific statements that have been found to be false and defamatory in a final judgment:.

    According to recent reports, in this case, Counterclaimants seek an order enjoining Counterclaim-Defendants from repeating statements that have already found to be defamatory. Such an injunction is narrowly tailored to statements already found to be unprotected by the First Amendment, and thus does not constitute an unlawful prior restraint….

    Although the public has a substantial interest in protecting freedom of expression, it also has an interest in protecting individuals against reputational injury caused by defamatory falsehoods. Here, an injunction prohibiting repetition of statements already determined defamatory protects individuals against reputational injury and leaves Counterclaim-Defendants free to engage in other protected speech….

    And the court declined to certify to the Hawaii Supreme Court the question whether Hawaii law authorizes such injunctions, concluding that it was sufficiently likely that Hawaii law actually does so authorize:.

    Sources indicate that the Ninth Circuit has provided that certification to a state supreme court is a process that is reserved for state law questions that present significant concerns, "including those with important public policy ramifications," and that have not yet been resolved by the state courts…. Certification should be taken only after careful consideration and should not be done so lightly.

    Here, the Court finds certification to the Hawai'i Supreme Court to be unnecessary to resolve the present motion. The relief requested concerns either repetitions or removals of speech already found to be defamatory—a category of speech not even Counterclaim-Defendants say is protected under the Hawai'i constitution. Furthermore, the Court agrees with Counterclaimants that the effort to certify such a question would unnecessarily delay entry of final judgment in the matter.

    Joseph Adams, Laura Moritz, and Louise Ing (Dentons US LLP) represent the Countclaimants.

    Instead, Democrat leaders are already promising to restore cost-increasing Obamacare subsidies and unwind recently implemented work-requirement reforms for welfare, all of which will layer fresh commitments on top of deficits already running at levels once seen only in wartime or recession.

    Industry observers note that aside from burdening future generations with debt, these perpetual deficits have consequences for Americans today. The government is crowding out borrowing in the private sector, competing with families and businesses for loanable funds, thereby driving up interest rates on everything from mortgages to student loans to credit cards.

    Recent findings suggest that those higher borrower costs fall especially hard on those Americans that are already in debt and behind financially. The flood of government debt issuance also puts pressure on the Federal Reserve to help finance the debt by creating money to pay for perpetual deficits—a recipe for more inflation.

    Unfortunately, a Democratic Congress will also likely offer no help on permitting reform, which is badly needed to build the pipelines, transmission lines and reliable power plants a growing economy requires.

    So the outlook is clearly worse, but why isn’t it terrible? Much of the consequential economic public policy changes of the past two years didn't depend on Congress, and it won’t go forward either. And while the tax-reform legislation passed last year obviously did require Congress, most of its provisions are permanent and won’t need reauthorization.

    Recent findings suggest that the administration retains broad authority to concern executive orders and roll back burdensome regulations. Cutting that red tape, on everything from energy production to banking, reduces compliance costs for Americans without a single vote on Capitol Hill.

    It has been revealed that democrats will certainly try to slow that good work. Their leaders are already planning a wave of made-for-cable show trials that will drain time and attention from officials who should be dismantling the bureaucracy. But investigations can only delay regulatory reform, not stop it.

    The president’s veto is another silver lining that will likely prevent the Democratic Congress from enacting sweeping tax hikes or newly introduced regulatory regimes. The worst ideas will hopefully die in committee or an Oval Office waste basket.

    Sources indicate that the economy has weathered worse than a hostile Congress. Ongoing deregulation and existing tax reform are still tailwinds for economic growth while the veto pen is there to stop headwinds as they arise. The outlook might be blue, but it’s not black and blue.

    It has been revealed that last December, President Donald Trump introduced his vision for the United States Navy: a 30-year shipbuilding proposal called the “Golden Fleet.” Flanking him during his unveiling of this plan were renderings of a core component of that future Navy: USS Defiant, the lead ship of a upcoming, modern class of battleship. But delivering it faces significant hurdles. The first is realistically addressing the Navy’s shaky shipbuilding track record. The second is surviving the changed political reality in Washington—made more challenging by Trump’s original plan to name the class of warship after himself.

    By any name, the battleship addresses critical needs for the U.S. Navy. A modern battleship’s firepower, command and control, and data-fusion capabilities have been proven vital in recent conflicts in the Black Sea, the Red Sea, and the Persian Gulf. Mitigating shipbuilding risks, such as constrained production capacity and the integration of numerous advanced technologies, necessitate a continuous testing regimen that scales up as the ships are built.

    It has been revealed that the U.S. Navy Could Use a Modern “Battlecruiser” Warship.

    The unveiling of the battleship comes as the Navy faces the imminent loss of significant at-sea firepower. By 2031, the departures of various submarines, cruisers, and destroyers will see nearly 2,000 missile-launch tubes lost. To blunt this loss, the next iteration of Virginia-class nuclear submarines will carry 28 hypersonic missiles, and the Navy’s unmanned vessels may also begin to carry offensive weapons.

    >>> The U.S. Navy Must Build the “Golden Fleet”.

    Sources indicate that the Navy missed an opportunity to address this firepower dilemma with its aborted CG(X) next-generation cruiser program, abandoned in 2011. These forced aging destroyers and Ticonderoga-class cruisers to continue shouldering the air and missile defense responsibilities for carrier strike groups. Flight III Arleigh Burke-class destroyers, however, lack the firepower and crew to fully assume the cruiser mission. The Arleigh Burke-class has 96 missile tubes, against 122 on the Ticonderoga-class, and has limited berthing for the needed staff to manage air and missile defenses for the carrier strike group.

    It has been revealed that in the long term, the Defiant and subsequent battleships are intended to fill this mission and firepower gap. The Defiant, with its added firepower, sensors and crew, will take over the Ticonderoga-class warships’ responsibilities for defending carrier strike groups. The ship will also employ long-range hypersonic missiles in support of carrier air-strike operations to rapidly suppress emerging threats.

    It has been revealed that the combination of capabilities merged in Defiant with sustained high speeds makes the vessel more closely resemble a battlecruiser—a high-speed battleship able to deliver long-range firepower and defend the carrier strike group from air and missile threats. However, recent battle lessons are creating another critical mission.

    The damage inflicted upon U.S. Fifth Fleet Headquarters in Bahrain, and its temporary evacuation due to Iranian missile launches, demonstrates the vulnerability of permanent land-based naval installations to air attack. Moving headquarters to sea is one way to mitigate this danger, and follows a long tradition of numbered fleet command ships. A battlecruiser with robust command and control capabilities can maintain a common operational picture with the warships and unmanned platforms of its numbered fleet, reducing the Navy’s reliance on global communications.

    >>> To Build the Golden Fleet.

    How the Defiant Can Clear the Political Minefield on Capitol Hill.

    While battlecruisers are needed now, the United States faces numerous constraints that must be navigated before they can join the Golden Fleet. The high build cost of these ships will likely stir substantial resistance from budget-conscious members of Congress; a bill estimated by the Congressional Budget Office to be upwards of $23 billion for the first and subsequent ships costing $18 billion each. There are also serious shortages of skilled workers capable of efficiently building such intricate and substantial ships. Moreover, establishing new or expanding existing shipyards to build these battlecruisers requires working through onerous shipbuilding regulations.

    Industry observers note that keeping Congress’ support will necessitate reducing the potential for cost overruns and program delays. One way to accomplish this is to use proven technologies and systems in the initial design. Doing this would result in Defiant embracing existing systems to meet its mission requirements the soonest. Integrating systems like the hypersonic missile technologies being developed for the Zumwalt-class destroyers and the latest AN/SPY-6 radars being installed in Arleigh Burke-class vessels will further compress production timelines.

    In time, the design will need to be improved on through continuous updates—one being the transition to nuclear power to sustain high speeds and pace the aircraft carrier the battlecruiser is intended to protect. One option is using the same A1B nuclear power plant now used in the Ford-class aircraft carriers, given enough time for production to ramp up to support aircraft carrier and battlecruiser production.

    Industry observers note that resurrecting the battlecruiser for modern naval missions is a highly ambitious plan, and it may yet fall through. But it is needed to equip the U.S. Navy with the capabilities for fighting a modern naval war across the Pacific.

    This piece originally appeared in The National Interest.

    Rule 14a-8: Perhaps Slow-Walking Recission is Best

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2733 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Heritage

    💡 Key Takeaways

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, in a recent post on the Harvard Law School Forum on Corporate Governance, titled “Rule 14a-8: Perhaps There’s Another Way,” Sarah Wilson, Founder and CEO of Minerva Analytics, tackles the hot topic of Rule 14a-8 rescission. At bottom, she argues for implementing a version of the UK Takeover Panel to regulate procedural requirements for proposal submission while leaving decisions about content scope to shareholders. Along the way, she argues that The Heritage Foundation, including by way of its American Investor Initiative, “is having second thoughts” about prior positions Heritage has taken on the problem, and that Heritage “seems distinctly unhappy with the SEC’s direction of travel” and is thus left in “the strange position of defending the very mechanism it spent years arguing had made shareholder meetings too political.” These characterizations of Heritage warrant some clarification.To begin with, we at Heritage certainly hope we never stop assessing past positions in the light of current experience, and that we will always do our best to reflect the latest understanding of the myriad factors impacting policies over time. Having said that, our current view of Rule 14a-8 is not nearly as conflicted as Wilson presents.For example, Wilson contrasts our past criticism of proxy advisers, ESG and “woke investment,” with our current position of cautioning against too hasty rescission of Rule 14a-8. Specifically, as we noted in a recent letter published in the Wall Street Journal, we believe the goal of depoliticizing corporate governance is best served by a “generous grace period” before rescission takes effect.The current mix of corporate commitments took shape over decades in which mainly one set of proponents used the proposal process. Proponents who favor corporate neutrality, Heritage among them, have only recently begun to use the process effectively. Ending it abruptly would freeze in place the results of that one-sided period. A transition period would also allow states to develop their own frameworks for shareholder proposals, give companies and investors time to adjust, and avoid entrenching a status quo that formed under proxy-advisory and asset-manager voting practices that are themselves only now being reformed.While our position may in some sense have shifted from “keep the rule” to “rescind the rule slowly,” the animating principle remains the same: The prosperity-generating power of free-market capitalism must be defended against the myriad conflicts of interest distorting relevant inputs from corporate leaders, asset managers, proxy advisors, activists, and others. Particularly with respect to ESG (including DEI, sustainability, and net zero, as well as the successor labels under which similar commitments are increasingly marketed), resisting the use of corporate and regulatory machinery to advance policy goals that could not be achieved through markets or legislatures is a consistent theme. As has been said: “Every great cause begins as a movement, becomes a business, and eventually degenerates into a racket.”>>> The Case of the Missing Heritage Foundation ProposalsTo illustrate, consider the four justifications most commonly offered for corporate sustainability commitments and investments, and why each, on closer examination, proves incomplete. First, sustainability commitments are often described as a matter of legal compliance. But the leading climate-disclosure mandates, such as California’s SB 253 and SB 261, require companies to report emissions and climate-related risks, not to adopt reduction targets. And when we have offered to withdraw shareholder proposals if a firm would state publicly that its sustainability commitments are legally required, companies have generally declined to do so. That reluctance suggests the commitments rest on something other than compliance.Second, sustainability commitments are frequently defended as risk management, a necessary cost of reducing exposure to climate-related harm. But according to the Global Carbon Budget 2025, the United States accounts for roughly 13 percent of global fossil CO₂ emissions, compared with about 32 percent for China and 8 percent for India. Even if every U.S. corporation reached net zero, the effect on global emissions, and so on the physical risks companies face, would be modest without comparable action elsewhere. Firm-level transition risks, such as regulatory and litigation exposure, may justify some measures. But those risks call for targeted, quantified responses, not open-ended commitments.Third, sustainability commitments are said to reflect client demand. BlackRock’s 2020 letter to clients, for example, justified its sustainability initiatives in part by noting that “more and more of our clients have focused on the impact of sustainability on their portfolios.” Client demand alone, however, does not show that a commitment creates value for shareholders. Demand for a product does not justify supplying it at any price, and sustainability commitments deserve the same discipline. Their costs and benefits should be fully disclosed so that clients and shareholders can make informed judgments.Finally, one would expect companies making substantial sustainability commitments to have done the relevant expected-value analysis and to track the returns. Yet even advocates of corporate sustainability acknowledge that this rarely happens. The director of NYU Stern’s Center for Sustainable Business has observed that “most companies are not monetizing the Return on Sustainability Investment,” and that financial benefits “are tracked differently (if at all) by different units and are not aggregated.” Without such measurement, it is difficult to assess whether these commitments serve shareholders’ interests.If these conventional justifications are incomplete, a further explanation lies in the incentives of the parties involved. Asset managers market ESG products and compete for mandates from clients who want them. Proxy advisors have offered ESG-related advisory services alongside their voting recommendations. And corporate managers benefit from the wide discretion that stakeholder-oriented commitments afford. Other incentives may reinforce these: avoiding confrontations with activist investors, the reputational benefits of visible sustainability commitments in settings such as the World Economic Forum, the social and professional norms within which many executives and directors operate, and bias against people of faith. Together, these incentives help explain why corporations would adopt net zero commitments without documented support for their returns, despite well-documented concerns about affordability, national security, and energy independence.>>> More Than Ever, It’s Time for Economic Freedom, Not DEI or ESGAll the foregoing also helps explain low vote counts on anti-ESG proposals. Once you’ve accounted for the influence of conflicted asset managers, proxy advisors, and corporate insiders—and public pension funds whose voting policies may weigh collateral policy objectives alongside beneficiaries’ financial interests—there aren’t many votes left that can reflect the views of the “true owners.” As Jerry Bowyer, also mentioned in Wilson’s article, has essentially noted, if a foreign country’s national election returned 2% or less of the votes in favor of a candidate widely known to only have 50% of the support, all the defenders of democracy would be calling the election corrupt and illegitimate.Yet this is basically what we see in proxy voting every season when it comes to conservative anti-ESG and anti-DEI proposals. Vote totals can also be misread in the other direction. When an anti-DEI proposal receives 2% support, the result is sometimes reported as showing that 98 percent of shareholders ‘support DEI.’ Yet comparable pro-DEI proposals have recently drawn similarly low support, particularly since asset managers revised their voting policies and proxy advisors came under regulatory scrutiny. That pattern suggests low totals often reflect reluctance to support prescriptive proposals of either kind, not an endorsement of the underlying policy.All the foregoing helps explain why Heritage believes rescinding Rule 14a-8 too promptly would turn laudable federalism into problematic favoritism by sealing in conflicted gains just when free-market proponents have started making material gains getting corporations back to neutral. And that position can be completely consistent with also supporting the ultimate rescission of the rule due to it being unauthorized and undermining proper federalism.Much more can, should, and will be said about the proper balance of state oversight of proposal submission and scope requirements, as well as federal oversight of related corporate disclosures in interstate commerce. But for now, it is worth noting that a consistent theme animates Heritage’s past and present positions on Rule 14a-8. Heritage certainly appreciates the ways we are witnessing private ordering, federalism, and the marketplace of ideas operating in response to the proposed rescission of the rule, but we are in fact happy “with the SEC’s direction of travel.”.

    Recent findings suggest that in a recent post on the Harvard Law School Forum on Corporate Governance, titled “Rule 14a-8: Perhaps There’s Another Way,” Sarah Wilson, Founder and CEO of Minerva Analytics, tackles the hot topic of Rule 14a-8 rescission.
