    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (Beirut) – Israeli authorities are detaining activists and community organizers attempting to protect Palestinian farmers during what the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) has recorded as the most violent West Bank olive harvest season in its 20 years of records, Human Rights Watch mentioned today.

    Industry observers note that between October 1 and 26, 2026, OCHA recorded 397 settler attacks resulting in casualties or property damage, the highest monthly figure it has recorded since its documentation began in 2006. Israeli soldiers were present in 26.5 percent of such incidents documented by the Israeli human rights organization Yesh Din between September 27 and October 14. The Israeli military has detained hundreds of people trying to protect Palestinian farmers during their harvest, according to local media reports.

    According to recent reports, “The olive harvest season should be a period of joy, strengthened community, and income for thousands of Palestinian families, but rising settler violence and harsh restrictions by the Israeli military have turned it into a period of anxiety and fear,” said Sarah Sanbar, acting Israel and Palestine director at Human Rights Watch. “Rather than stopping settler violence, the Israeli military is detaining the people trying to ensure that Palestinian farmers can safely harvest their olives.”.

    Recent findings suggest that human Rights Watch interviewed four activists organizing groups or volunteers protecting Palestinians harvesting their olives, two of whom had been detained and released since 2025. Human Rights Watch wrote to the Israeli military on November 16; its responses are reflected below.

    Settler violence in the West Bank has been steadily rising since the current Netanyahu government took office in December 2022. Settlers responsible for attacks operate with the financial, material, and legal backing of the Israeli state. Attacks by armed settlers often occur alongside Israeli army units or with soldiers standing by.

    Absent state protection, Palestinian communities and activists have organized to protect themselves using a tactic called protective presence. This is a form of nonviolent activism and human rights monitoring where international, Israeli, and Palestinian volunteers physically accompany vulnerable communities.

    “[Their presence helps] to deter settlers, or have less violent attacks, and speed up the harvest so people do not have to stay for long exposed in the areas,” Rabie Abu Naim, a Palestinian farmer and activist from Al-Mughayyir village, northeast of Ramallah, told Human Rights Watch.

    In a recent development, however, the international presence is no longer able to deter settler attacks, or the military’s obstruction of the harvest. “I have been doing this for more than ten years,” an organizer said. “What we used to think could protect farmers no longer works. Since 2023, all red lines have been crossed.”.

    Abu Naim described recent attacks by settlers in Al-Mughayyir, including beatings, burning cars, use of tear gas, and stopping cars on the road: “Anyone who takes the road to Abu-Falah on the western side of the village, which is now the only entry to Al-Mughayyir, says their shahada [the Islamic declaration of faith, said as final words before dying]. They are entering an ambush … they either survive or they don’t.”.

    “This year’s olive harvest season is one of the worst that Al-Mughayyir ever knew,” Abu Naim noted. “[Settler attacks] are becoming an hourly thing, not daily.”.

    According to recent reports, abu Naim was arrested in October 2025 and administratively detained for nine months. “I suspect it was because of coordinating [protection during] the olive harvest season,” he noted.

    Al-Mughayyir’s farmers have been steadily losing access to their olive groves. In August 2025, the head of the Israeli military’s Central Command signed an order for the uprooting of olive trees on 300 dunams (30 hectares) of land in Al-Mughayyir, ostensibly for security reasons after a Palestinian reportedly shot and wounded a settler who had trespassed on the village’s land. According to Israeli human rights group Kerem Navot, settlers from the Shiloh area carried out clearing operations on about 620 dunams (62 hectares), more than twice the area covered by the order, then took over parts of the land.

    In a recent development, “This year, there are no [protection] campaigns for Al-Mughayyir, because there are no lands we can access,” Abu Naim said. “This year’s season, we can say that there isn’t a harvest.”.

    The Israeli human rights organization Peace Now reported in October that the Israeli military had signed orders barring Palestinians from entering approximately 88,300 dunams (around 21,800 acres) of land in the West Bank, 30 percent more than in 2025, unless they coordinate with the military in advance. The military barred Israeli citizens from only 6,890 dunams of West Bank land, Peace Now reported.

    Industry observers note that the Israeli army routinely designates areas as “closed military zones” to forbid Palestinian farmers and international activists from accessing their lands. Legally, this means the land is entirely closed to Palestinians unless authorized by the military. Those entering their fields without prior coordination are committing a criminal offence under Israeli law and face potential removal or arrest.

    Sources indicate that community organizers remarked, though, that coordinating with the military does not always guarantee their security. “For Area C [i.e. areas under full Israeli security control and civil administration], it is completely forbidden to go, even if we do the necessary coordination,” Abu Naim said. “If we get there with the coordination then settlers come, they provoke, attack, call the army and tell them they’re being attacked, so the army comes and clears the area.”.

    Activists said that the military has claimed certain land is a “closed military zone” without providing documentation, to deter farmers and activists from reaching the olive groves. “They came to us and asked us to leave because we are in a closed military zone,” said Matten Kadish-Berner, an Israeli activist and organizer with Protect the Harvest. “When we asked them to show us the order, they refused, and in the end, they left because they did not have any document.”.

    The Israeli military told Human Rights Watch that the designation of closed military zones is intended to “prevent friction and public order disturbances,” noting that this year, “ahead of the harvest, a dedicated harvest situation room was established for the first time in the Civil Administration.”.

    Israeli authorities routinely intimidate and arrest Palestinians and deport international activists engaged in organizing protection for Palestinian farmers during olive harvest season.

    On October 27, Israeli soldiers raided Burin village, south of Nablus, and detained about 60 people, said the Sumood Network, a Palestinian grassroots organization. All were released except Ghassan Najjar, a farmer and rights defender who co-founded the Sumood Network.

    The Sumood Network said that before the season began, security agents from the Shin Bet threatened to detain Najjar if he continued to coordinate protection for the olive harvest in the Nablus area.

    On November 17, an Israeli judge approved a four-month administrative detention order for Najjar, the Sumood Network remarked. During the judicial review, the Israeli Military Prosecution acknowledged that the administrative detention of Najjar is related to political activities that are unarmed and nonviolent, the Sumood Network said. The Israeli military said Najjar “is suspected of hurling stones at Israeli civilians,” which the Sumood Network disputed.

    Israeli authorities often detain Palestinians on the basis of secret evidence that neither the detainee nor their lawyer can see. Orders last up to six months and can be renewed repeatedly, with no limit. International law allows detention without trial only as an exceptional measure, for imperative security reasons, with impartial judicial review. When it is used routinely, it becomes a tool of punishment and control and therefore arbitrary and unlawful.

    According to the Israeli organization HaMoked, Israel held 3,101 Palestinians in administrative detention as of October.

    On October 21, the military detained about 80 US, Israeli, and British volunteers helping Palestinians harvest olives near Bethlehem, including now US Congressman-elect Brad Lander, several rabbis, and Israel’s former deputy attorney general. A few days earlier, Israeli settlers attacked a delegation of French, Belgian, and Polish diplomats, Catholic clergymen, and a French mayor.

    Israeli authorities should release all those held unlawfully under administrative detention, end the systematic use of administrative detention, and ensure Palestinian farmers can safely reach their land.

    Other countries should act to prevent further atrocities across the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including by imposing targeted sanctions on those implicated in ongoing grave abuses, suspending arms transfers to Israel, banning trade with illegal settlements, considering suspending preferential trade agreements with Israel, and supporting the International Criminal Court and its ongoing investigations, including by executing its arrest warrants.

    “Organizing an olive harvest is not a crime,” Sanbar remarked. “Israeli authorities should end their repression of activists and instead fulfill their obligations to protect the Palestinian population.”.

    November 23, 2026: This news release has been updated to clarify which activists were released following the October 27 raid in Burin village.

    Some Miscellaneous SCOTUS Scoops From Woodward's "Secret"

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1496 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that bob Woodward's upcoming book is a bit unusual.
    • According to recent reports, beyond any particulars about the Justices, I found most insightful his craft in getting people to speak.
    • Scott and I were intensely pursuing interviews with clerks all over the country.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that bob Woodward's upcoming book is a bit unusual. There is no coherent narrative or flow. Each chapter simply tells the story of another one of his sources. Chapters 36 through 43 walk through his interviews with Supreme Court Justices, law clerks, and others for The Brethren. The book is a collection of his recollections, mostly from recorded memos, and what all of his source said.

    According to recent reports, beyond any particulars about the Justices, I found most insightful his craft in getting people to speak. He invariably starts by finding someone low on the totem pole, building trust, and working his way up.

    Scott and I were intensely pursuing interviews with clerks all over the country. The names of all the law clerks, past and present, was readily available public information. I cannot underscore enough how important it is in journalism to focus on the low end of the totem pole. Presidents, justices, cabinet officials are all important interviews.

    What began as a somewhat random "catch-as-catch-can" for Scott and me helped us get inside, as we used what we collected to dig deeper. Quoting information or documents we already possessed helped give confidence to other clerks who would then sometimes reach into their own archives to add details and documents. . . .

    Most of the information in our book, The Brethren, is based on interviews with more than 200 people, including five justices who talked, 170 former and current law clerks, and several dozen former employees of the court. Virtually all the interviews were conducted on deep background, meaning that the identity of the sources would be kept confidential for their lifetimes but all the information could be used in the book. Since all of the justices are now deceased, I am lifting the lid on our interviews with them.

    Industry observers note that this sort of journalism takes time and time and more time. But eventually, he has enough information that principals feel comfortable talking to him. And even if he learned what happened from multiple sources, asking yet another source opens up the possibility for even more insights to be gleaned.

    Sources indicate that chapter 36 recounts Woodward's interactions with Justice Stewart, who invited the reporter to his home for an interview. Stewart spoke very critically of Chief Justice Burger. That interview convinced Woodward there was enough to write a book. The publisher gave him and Scott Armstrong a $300,000 advance. That is more than $1.5 million in present-day value.

    Chapter 37 recounts Woodward's interview with Justice Powell. Powell invited him to the Court—right away. Woodward arrived at 4:30 p.m. that day. Powell said, "Intellectually there is no Brandeis or Frankfurter or Cardozo on the court now." I've made similar comments since Justice Scalia's passing. I wonder if any members of the current Court think they are at the intellectual level of Holmes or Story? I appreciate Powell's humility.

    Woodward would interview Powell two more times. I found these comments about Roe striking:.

    In a recent development, I asked him about the Supreme Court's landmark 1973 abortion decisions in Roe v. Wade and Doe v. Bolton, which legalized abortion nationwide. "It was hard for me and I was frankly strongly result oriented," Powell mentioned of the decision. "I would support abortion funding by the states if I was in the legislature," he added. This caught me off-guard and seemed contrary to the opinions he had written saying there was no right to a state-funded abortion.

    It has been revealed that "I thought the abortion laws were atrocious," Powell continued, referring to the state abortion laws prohibiting abortion. "If you wanted to pay for an abortion you could get one." I noted his selection of the word "wanted" instead of "could afford" which was a massive part of the issue as I saw it.

    According to recent reports, there should be no doubt that Roe was an outcome-driven decision. There was no law—just policy.

    Chapter 38 focuses on how he interviewed more than 170 law clerks. Powell authorized his law clerks to speak to Woodward. Burger's former clerks were "at times the most helpful," especially since Woodward never bothered asking Burger to speak. I already recounted the story in which he "borrowed" Justice Brennan's history of the Watergate tape case.

    Chapter 39 explains how Justice Powell thought the Justices should talk to reporters to minimize the bad press. Powell wrote in a draft letter to Burger that he never sent: "I had rather someone on the Court discussed this with him accurately than leave him to reach his own conclusions with the right to say that he was stonewalled by the Justices.".

    Recent findings suggest that chapter 40 discusses Armstrong's interview with Justice Blackmun, and the resulting "19-page single-spaced memo." There were a few useful nuggets. Blackmun appreciated how he wasn't Nixon's first or even second choice for the seat.

    "I am humbled by the fact that I was number three, not the number one choice," Blackmun said of his appointment to the Supreme Court. Nixon's first choice, Clement Haynsworth, a federal judge from South Carolina, and second choice, G. Harrold Carswell, a federal judge from Florida, were rejected narrowly in brutal public fights, largely over concerns that Nixon was attempting to shift the court's ideology, which of course he was. Blackmun had been confirmed unanimously in May 1970 in a 94-to-0 vote. "A scarecrow could get nominated after what had happened," Blackmun continued. "It was a difficult period for the Senate. A number of [senators] told me that they wanted to get it over with. They had a real sense of relief that an average guy had come along with whom they couldn't find much wrong.".

    I wonder if Justice Kennedy ever had similar marks of humility, as a fellow third-choice?

    Blackmun was also assigned the Roe opinion because Chief didn't want to take the heat:.

    Blackmun said he was well aware that no matter what he wrote, the opinion would be controversial and he would be hated and vilified. The chief could not afford to take on such a controversial case himself, particularly from the minority. "That's why I was assigned the abortion memo. We were scattered on it," Blackmun said. Douglas was the court's mischievous liberal, the rebel, and couldn't be the author. Any abortion opinion Douglas wrote would be widely questioned outside the court. Brennan was a firm vote for striking down the state abortion laws, but he was the court's only sitting Catholic. As such, Brennan could not be expected to take the heat from the Catholic anti-abortion groups. Marshall could not author for similar reasons: An opinion by the court's only Black man could be perceived as specifically designed for Black people or incite race-fueled blame for the decision. Stewart would have trouble going very far… That left one option: Blackmun.

    According to recent reports, by Chapter 41, the first draft of the book was complete. Now, Powell declined to talk further with Woodward.

    Chapter 42 recounts a fairly gruff interview with Justice White, who gave up virtually nothing.

    Industry observers note that chapter 43 relays how Justice Powell wrote to Chief Justice Burger about the newly introduced book. Powell, of course, did not disclose how he spoke with Woodward, and how he authorized his clerks to do the same. I can get Burger's frustration.

    It has been revealed that chief Justice Warren Burger erupted in a letter back to Powell, squarely blaming the clerks and noting "there are hazards in talking with certain 'categories' in this life"—meaning me and Scott, or reporters in general. He criticized the clerks for seeming to have succumbed to the "glamour" of rubbing shoulders with "print names!" . . .

    I wondered if Burger knew that five of the seven justices in his ranks had talked to us and several had given their clerks permission to assist us.

    If only Burger knew that Powell and others blabbed. I suspect Chief Justice Roberts can relate.

    It also turns out that Woodward asked a young Stephen Breyer to fact-check the book.

    Recent findings suggest that another secret that has a certain historic value today was that one weekend before The Brethren went to the printers, a young man named Stephen Breyer came over to my home. He sat in the living room and read the book cover to cover. At that time he was chief counsel to the Senate Judiciary Committee chaired by Senator Ted Kennedy. Scott had insisted we have the book's use of legal terms checked for obvious errors. After reading, Breyer told us it was "a hell of a book.".

    I would note there is no discussion of interviewing Justice Rehnquist, even though Rehnquist is named as a source. Something is off.

    Industry observers note that that's it. Nothing earth-shattering. But it is a shame Woodward decided to relay non-public communications with Breyer and Kagan, who are both alive and well.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The French Senate on November 20 approved a controversial bill that risks deepening impunity for use of lethal force by police.

    The bill introduces a legal presumption of self-defense for law enforcement officers using firearms during the exercise of their duties, unless victims or their families can establish the use of lethal force was unlawful.

    Because victims’ families lack access to key evidence to assess the legality of police-caused death, placing the burden of proof on them is likely to deepen impunity and seriously jeopardize pathways for accountability where lethal force was unlawful, unnecessary, or disproportionate. This is inconsistent with France’s human rights obligations with respect to protecting the right to life and use of force by law enforcement.

    The use of lethal force by police is a major concern in France. In 2023, a police officer fatally shot 17-year-old Nahel M., a racialized boy, during a traffic stop, triggering widespread scrutiny of police use of firearms.

    France’s national human rights body and the previous mandate holder of the independent ombudsperson as well as a United Nations rights expert raised serious rights concerns about the bill, while rights groups, activists, and legal professionals staged protests and petitioned parliament to stop the bill.

    In a recent development, the Senate’s vote followed approval of the bill by France’s National Assembly on July 7. Unless government officials or parliamentarians refer the bill for constitutional review, the president has 15 days to sign it into law.

    Since 2017, when lawmakers broadened the scope of permissible use of firearms by police well beyond international human rights standards requiring necessity and proportionality, numbers of fatal police vehicle stops in France have risen fivefold compared to before.

    Industry observers note that A state cannot delegate its legal duty to investigate to those affected by lethal police force. This reversed burden of proof contravenes international human rights law, which requires states to thoroughly investigate every circumstance of lethal police force.

    If the French authorities are serious about avoiding incidents of excessive use of lethal force, and rebuilding public confidence in policing, lawmakers should drop this bill. The government and parliament should instead focus legislative efforts on strengthening accountability and ensuring that police powers are subject to effective procedural safeguards to protect people from police abuse, discrimination, violence, and, increasingly, disproportionate use of firearms.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A recent Fresh York City law banning horse-drawn carriages is unconstitutional, according to a federal lawsuit filed Thursday by a union that represents carriage owners and operators. (Photo from Shutterstock).

    A recent Upcoming York City law banning horse-drawn carriages is unconstitutional, according to a federal lawsuit filed Thursday by a union that represents carriage owners and operators.

    According to recent reports, the city council passed the ban Thursday, putting an end to a 168-year industry that has attracted a healthy tourist business. Newly introduced York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani plans to sunset the carriages by June 1, 2028, in all five boroughs in the city. The union representing carriage operators and owners argues that their livelihood has been taken away and seeks to have the ban struck down.

    “The city’s approach can be summarized in 12 words: immediately cripple the owners, ignore property interests and contracts, and maybe compensate,” according to the suit.

    Additionally, the newly introduced law stipulates the “humane disposition” of the horses. Animal rights activists have in the past expressed concern over the welfare of the horses. Earlier this year, an 18-year-old tourist died after jumping from a runaway carriage—the first fatality since the carriages were introduced into Central Park in New York City.

    “Our city has changed, and now it is time for our laws to change, too,” Mamdani said.

    Bloomberg Law and MSN had coverage.

    #124473. Tech Report: Quorums in Times of Crisis

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1555 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Reason ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: Quorums in Times of Crisis

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1555 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that last week the Fifth Circuit ruled that the House's proxy-quorum policy violated the Quorum Clause.
    • Much of the doomsaying is out of proportion to reality.
    • According to recent reports, perhaps the only major outlier is the Electoral Count Reform Act.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that last week the Fifth Circuit ruled that the House's proxy-quorum policy violated the Quorum Clause. I've yet to read any actual substantive disagreements with the merits. Rather, there have been a smattering of warnings about the potential consequences of the decision, attacks on the Fifth Circuit's track record in past cases, and predictive judgments about what the Supreme Court will do. I assure you. If you actually read the Fifth Circuit's decision and the dissent, there is not even a close call. Unless consequentialism matters more than originalism.

    Much of the doomsaying is out of proportion to reality. In order for anyone to challenge a federal statute passed during this period, they would need to have both a reason and standing. Litigation is expensive and time-consuming. Parties do not simply file lawsuits for principle. Again, any remedy would be targeted to a particular law, so it is not possible to wipe out all legislation from this period. The courts do not have a magic eraser for the U.S. Code. Moreover, spending bills and related laws generally do not inflict injuries, so there is no obvious way to challenge many of the bills. Remember that Judge Hendrix found that Texas lacked standing to challenge the DHS Pilot Program, another proxy-passed-statute.

    According to recent reports, perhaps the only major outlier is the Electoral Count Reform Act. The validity of this statute would only arise in the case of a contested election. There is good reason to have the validity of this law settled. But there is an easy path forward. This was a bipartisan statute that could be re-enacted to eliminate any doubts.

    You might say it is unfair to make Congress re-enact a bill it already passed. I have zero sympathy for the House, which passed a landmark piece of legislation in the face of serious constitutional doubts. There was no actual health emergency that required the rule. The House could have easily followed social distancing protocols to allow members to spread out. The gallery upstairs would serve that purpose well.

    It has been revealed that the House also could have opened a Zoom link for those who are unable to attend. Had these members been able to watch and participate in the proceedings and cast their vote at the time of the roll call, the legal issue would have been much closer. In February 2021, I participated as a virtual witness for Merrick Garland's confirmation hearing. It could be done. Senators who were in the chamber posed questions that I was able to answer.

    In a recent development, the purpose of a deliberative body is to allow members to vote after open deliberation. Designating a vote in advance of the proceeding eliminates any chance for deliberation. Even in my own world, I often walk into a faculty meeting thinking I'll vote one way on a matter, but after hearing other views, I change my position.

    Recent findings suggest that I suspect others can relate. The Supreme Court satisfied its statutory quorum requirement through remote oral argument. No one would have thought that Chief Justice Roberts could have sat alone in the Chamber, posing the questions that his colleagues sent in advance. Absent Justices could not submit signed proxy votes in advance of the oral argument that would be read aloud at conference. The same rules ought to apply to Congress.

    The truth is the proxy rule was more about Speaker Pelosi's power than actual pandemic relief. As I noted, I have no sympathy when Congress takes shortcuts. Courts with jurisdiction have an unflagging duty to exercise it. And all of the usual presumptions in favor of democracy do not apply when the legislative body ignores the bright-line procedural rules in the constitution. If INS v. Chadha was right--even though the heavens fell--then the quorum case is even righter.

    Recent findings suggest that what matters to me are originalist principles. And the good judges of the Fifth Circuit followed the law where it leads. They were not cowed by potential consequences in other cases and the predictable hackles from commentators.

    In a recent development, I've started to give the matter a bit more thought, and researched past instances in American history where Congress somehow managed to legislate during times of actual crisis. Here are four highlights.

    Sources indicate that in August 1793, a yellow fever epidemic began to spread through Philadelphia—then the capital of the United States. At the time, Congress was in recess, and it was believed that holding meetings in the capital, including meetings of the legislature, would be unsafe. For that reason, President George Washington asked both James Madison and Thomas Jefferson whether he could summon—in effect, order—Congress to meet in a different location. They both advised that the President lacked the power to change the location of the meeting, but they proposed alternatives. Madison advised that Washington could suggest that the members meet him in nearby Lancaster or Reading, Pennsylvania. Jefferson insisted that Congress "must meet in Philadelphia, "even if it be in the open fields, to adjourn themselves to some other place." I am not aware of any evidence that either Jefferson or Madison or any of their peers ever considered the possibility that the Constitution's quorum rule could be relaxed in order to allow members to establish their presence or otherwise participate by proxy.

    Sources indicate that on August 8, 1814, about two weeks before the British would invade Washington, the national capital, and then burn the Capitol, President James Madison called on Congress to convene on September 19. Congress, unwilling to be defeated, found temporary accommodations in the Patent and Post Office Building (now the site of the National Portrait Gallery). Despite the risks of public safety, nearly 90% of the representatives were present. Again, there were no efforts to relax the Constitution's quorum rule, and there were no attempts to facilitate proxies as a means of carrying on legislative business.

    In a recent development, during the American Civil War, debates about the quorum proved particularly vexing by 1864. Should Representatives and Senators from States that took action to join the (purported) Confederate States of America be counted for purposes of a quorum? Ultimately, Senators from the Union States adopted a rule such that quorum was defined as "a majority of the Senators duly chosen." Because the southern state legislatures had not chosen new Senators for the United States Congress, vacancies for authorized senate seats were not filled, and so no one was "duly chosen." Thus, such authorized seats did not count for purposes of the quorum. I do not believe that this rule was an innovation, much less a relaxation of the quorum rule. Rather, the Senate's rule merely clarified the constitutional text and was entirely consistent with prior practice going back to 1790, when the Second Session of the Senate of the First Congress met. Moreover, the Civil War era congresses did not introduce any form of proxy voting.

    In 1918, the Spanish influenza raged through the United States. It is understood that more than one-half million people in the United States would die from this epidemic. The Senate had passed a resolution to authorize the President to appoint certain medical professionals to the Public Health Service. The House, however, lacked a quorum to act, and the Speaker adjourned that day's meeting. The following day, the members worked out a one-time "gentleman's agreement" where no one would object to the lack of a quorum; absent a timely objection by a member in attendance the chair would presume the presence of a quorum. The bill passed under these somewhat unusual parliamentary circumstances, which the House would not repeat during the remainder of the epidemic. There was no attempt to allow absent members to designate a proxy to vote for them. Moreover, the constitutionality of this practice was never tested in court. I agree with Judge Hendrix's take on the Spanish Influenza incident:.

    In a recent development, this occurrence does not support an argument that the Quorum Clause does not require physical presence. Quite the opposite, the House was aware it lacked a quorum at the time, with members urging those who considered raising points of no quorum to withdraw their points because they knew a quorum call would reveal the obvious—the House lacked the physical presence of a quorum and therefore could not proceed to business. And the members sought to pass the bill by unanimous consent because a roll-call vote would reveal the absence of a quorum. The House's decision to proceed in knowing violation of a constitutional requirement does not alter the proper interpretation of that Clause—"[p]ast practice does not, by itself, create power." See Medellín v. Texas, 552 U.S. 491, 532 (2008) (alteration in original) (quoting Dames & Moore v. Regan, 453 U.S. 654, 686 (1981)). Instead, it may merely represent action beyond constitutional authority. But given the House's own acknowledgement at the time and the history previously discussed, the historical practice of the House—even when acting without a quorum—demonstrates an understanding that members must be physically present in order to count towards the quorum.

    Industry observers note that I thank Professor Seth Barrett Tillman for his help with this post. Seth's essay on the Quorum Clause for the Heritage Guide to the Constitution is well worth reading.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Azerbaijan’s parliament on November 18 approved sweeping amendments to legislation governing nongovernmental organizations (NGOs) that would expand government powers to suspend and dissolve independent groups, impose new registration requirements, and further restrict their operations.
    • The proposed legislation would allow authorities, rather than courts, to suspend NGOs for up to a year for broadly defined violations, including failure to meet transparency and anti-money laundering requirements.
    • Existing NGOs would have just 30 days after the law takes effect to revise their charters and apply for re-registration.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Azerbaijan’s parliament on November 18 approved sweeping amendments to legislation governing nongovernmental organizations (NGOs) that would expand government powers to suspend and dissolve independent groups, impose new registration requirements, and further restrict their operations. The following day, a court sentenced prominent rights defender Bashir Suleymanli to seven and a half years in prison, the latest in a series of harsh sentences against civil society activists prosecuted over foreign funding.

    The proposed legislation would allow authorities, rather than courts, to suspend NGOs for up to a year for broadly defined violations, including failure to meet transparency and anti-money laundering requirements. It would also expand grounds for court-ordered dissolution to include activities deemed a threat to the “legally protected interests of the state and society”—vague standards open to abuse.

    Existing NGOs would have just 30 days after the law takes effect to revise their charters and apply for re-registration. The minimum capital to establish a nonprofit foundation, a type of nongovernmental organization, would increase tenfold, from 10,000 to 100,000 manats (approx. US$ 59,000). Together, these requirements would create additional barriers to establishing and maintaining independent civil society organizations in Azerbaijan.

    Human Rights Watch has documented how existing restrictions on registration and foreign funding have forced many independent groups to close or severely curtail their activities. The European Court of Human Rights has repeatedly found violations of freedom of association in cases involving Azerbaijani civil society organizations.

    Authorities took another strike at civil society on November 19 when the Baku Grave Crimes Court convicted Suleymanli, director of the Institute for Citizens’ Rights, of apparent politically motivated charges of money laundering and abuse of office. Arrested in March 2025, authorities prosecuted Suleymanli as part of a reopened investigation into foreign-funded NGO work.

    Industry observers note that courts have also handed down lengthy prison sentences to other activists prosecuted in connection with the same investigation, including eight years for Asaf Ahmadov and seven years and three months for Zamin Zaki (Zakiyev). Election monitor Anar Mammadli received a 13-year sentence in September following an unfair trial.

    Azerbaijani authorities should withdraw the proposed amendments, release Suleymanli and other civil society activists imprisoned for their legitimate work, and end the misuse of criminal law against independent groups. Azerbaijan’s international partners should press the government to uphold its obligations to protect freedom of association.

    Virginia S. Ct.: Felons Who Served Their Sentences Regain Second Amendment Rights Unless …

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2720 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • From today's long decision of the Virginia Supreme Court in Ginevan v.
    • On January 24, 2023, police responded to a possible domestic disturbance where they encountered Ginevan in a dispute with a woman.
    • It has been revealed that A review of Ginevan's prior criminal history revealed various and sundry felony convictions.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    From today's long decision of the Virginia Supreme Court in Ginevan v. Commonwealth, written by Justice Wesley Russell:.

    On January 24, 2023, police responded to a possible domestic disturbance where they encountered Ginevan in a dispute with a woman. The woman claimed that Ginevan had grabbed a shotgun and pointed it at her. Although Ginevan admitted to possessing the shotgun, he denied having pointed it at the woman. He told police that he had the shotgun for protection. After Ginevan confirmed that he was a convicted felon, he was arrested and charged with possessing a firearm as a convicted felon in violation of Code § 18.2-308.2.

    It has been revealed that A review of Ginevan's prior criminal history revealed various and sundry felony convictions. In 2011, Ginevan was convicted of possession with intent to distribute a Schedule I/II controlled substance. Over the following four years, he was convicted three times for felony probation violations. Then, in 2018, Ginevan was convicted of obtaining money by false pretenses as well as possession of ammunition by a convicted felon. Notably, pursuant to Code § 17.1-805(C), the General Assembly has classified possession of ammunition by a convicted felon as a violent felony, but none of Ginevan's other felony convictions are so classified.

    Recent findings suggest that the court held that the Virginia statute banning felons from possessing guns was unconstitutional as applied to Ginevan. Some brief excerpts from the long opinion:.

    Sources indicate that beginning with its decision in Heller, the Supreme Court has often included statements in its Second Amendment cases suggesting that bans on previously convicted felons possessing firearms were acceptable or, at the very least, that nothing in its decisions should be read as addressing felon-in-possession bans. For example, in Heller, the majority stated that.

    nothing in our opinion should be taken to cast doubt on longstanding prohibitions on the possession of firearms by felons and the mentally ill, or laws forbidding the carrying of firearms in sensitive places such as schools and government buildings, or laws imposing conditions and qualifications on the commercial sale of arms….

    Critically, however, these statements about dispossessing felons all were made in cases where the question of whether the Second Amendment allowed legislatures to forever bar felons from possessing firearms was not an issue…. As such, the statements about felon-in-possession bans contained in these cases are properly understood as dicta and not holdings of the Supreme Court….

    In a recent development, in Bruen, … the Supreme Court set forth an analytical framework that courts must apply in evaluating Second Amendment challenges to limitations on a person's right to keep and bear arms. In explaining the framework, the Supreme Court wrote that.

    we hold that when the Second Amendment's plain text covers an individual's conduct, the Constitution presumptively protects that conduct. To justify its regulation, the government may not simply posit that the regulation promotes an important interest. Rather, the government must demonstrate that the regulation is consistent with this Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation. Only if a firearm regulation is consistent with this Nation's historical tradition may a court conclude that the individual's conduct falls outside the Second Amendment's "unqualified command." ….

    In a recent development, our conclusion that the Bruen framework and not the Heller dicta provides the rule of decision does not answer the question of whether or not, as applied to Ginevan, Code § 18.2-308.2 violates the Second Amendment. Rather, it requires that we apply the framework to Ginevan's conviction and circumstances as revealed by the record in this case….

    According to recent reports, [T]he first part of the Bruen framework requires that we determine whether Code § 18.2-308.2's prohibition conflicts with the text of the Second Amendment. To answer this question, the Supreme Court counsels asking three "subsidiary questions": (1) "[D]oes the law apply to 'the people?'"; (2) Does the law apply to Second Amendment "[a]rms, i.e., any weapon customarily used for offensive or defensive purposes?"; and (3) Does the law restrict a person's ability to keep or bear an arm that is protected by the Second Amendment?

    In this case, there has not and cannot be any dispute that the second and third questions must be answered in the affirmative. The weapon Ginevan is charged for possessing is an ordinary shotgun, which clearly falls within the scope of a weapon in common use for lawful purposes. {Although there is evidence in this case that Ginevan may have pointed his shotgun at someone, he was neither charged with nor convicted for any use of the shotgun. He was charged only with mere possession, so our review is focused on whether the Commonwealth may ban his possession of a firearm.} Accordingly, it unquestionably is an arm for the purposes of the Second Amendment.

    Industry observers note that similarly, because Code § 18.2-308.2 is a blanket ban on Ginevan even possessing such a shotgun, there can be no question that it restricts his ability to keep and bear arms. Thus, the only inquiry from Bruen's first step that could even be in dispute is whether Ginevan's prior felony convictions removed him from "the people" protected by the Second Amendment….

    Starting with Heller and continuing in more recent cases, the United States Supreme Court has indicated that "the people" protected by the Second Amendment includes "all members of the political community[.]" … The fact that the phrase "right of the people" means the same thing in the First, Fourth, and Second Amendments is, by our reckoning, sufficient to resolve whether a felony conviction, without more, removes a person from the political community.

    It almost goes without saying that no one would contend that, once convicted of a felony, a non-incarcerated person would fall outside the protections of the First Amendment, and therefore no longer enjoy "the right of the people peaceably to assemble, and to petition the Government for a redress of grievances." Similarly, no one maintains that a felony conviction forever forfeits "[t]he right of the people to be secure in their persons, houses, papers, and effects, against unreasonable searches and seizures[.]"Because a felony conviction does not remove a person from "the people" referenced in the First and Fourth Amendments, we conclude that, as a matter of language and logic, it does not remove a person from "the people" referenced in the Second Amendment.

    In a recent development, of course, our conclusion that Ginevan is not excluded from "the people" referenced in the Second Amendment represents the beginning and not the end of the analysis. As then-Judge Barrett observed, the conclusion that felons do not fall outside the Second Amendment "does not mean that the government cannot prevent them from possessing guns. Instead, it means that the question is whether the government has the power to disable the exercise of a right that they otherwise possess, rather than whether they possess the right at all." Accordingly, we now turn to Bruen's second step and whether the Commonwealth had the power to disable Ginevan's exercise of his rights under the Second Amendment….

    [1.] Lack of an historical twin.

    Although governments are not required to prove the existence of an historical twin from the relevant historical period to justify a modern regulation, the existence or absence of one certainly is something to consider…. Statutes banning convicted felons from possessing firearms as a result of their prior felony convictions are a creature of twentieth century legislatures. When asked at oral argument, the Commonwealth could not identify a single American statute that banned all convicted felons from possessing firearms that predated the federal effort in the 1960s….

    [2.] Felon punishment at the time of the Founding.

    It has been revealed that the Commonwealth argues that a total ban on felons possessing firearms is permissible because, at the time of the Founding, felonies routinely warranted "punishments far harsher than disarmament, including execution, estate forfeiture, or life imprisonment. And if the greater punishment of death and estate forfeiture was permissible to punish felons, then the lesser restriction of permanent disarmament is also permissible." … Although this approach provides a reasonably clear rule of decision and has some facial appeal, we, for the reasons detailed below, do not believe it withstands scrutiny….

    It has been revealed that the argument has its genesis in the English common law and how felons were punished. In England prior to the Founding, felonies often were punished by death and estate forfeiture. Before the sentence of death was actually carried out or in the instances in which a sentence of less than death was imposed, the convicted person was subject to attainder. Attainder was the common law process "of extinguishing a person's civil rights when that person is sentenced to death or declared an outlaw for committing a felony or treason." It inflicted what has been called civil death or civiliter mortuus, rendering the person as devoid of rights as if he were actually dead.

    It has been revealed that although the recognized process in England, not all aspects of the process were adopted in the colonies or in the nascent American republic. In his treatise on Blackstone's Commentaries, St. George Tucker noted that "[c]onfiscations, forfeitures, and corruption of blood, do not follow in case of conviction or attainder for any treason or felony either in the commonwealth of Virginia, or under the federal government." … By the late 1800s, multiple courts, including this one, explicitly recognized that, to the extent that civil death existed in America, it was temporary and ended when the convict had completed any period of incarceration….

    Not only do we find that the historical practice does not support the Commonwealth's argument regarding Second Amendment rights, but we reject the logical endpoint of the Commonwealth's argument. If the greater potential punishment of death allowed for all lesser punishments, including the stripping of Second Amendment rights, it also allowed for the stripping of all other constitutional rights. After all, the Supreme Court has made clear that the Second Amendment right is not a lesser right and is of equal dignity as the other rights elucidated in the Bill of Rights.

    Just as a dead man cannot keep and bear arms, he cannot freely exercise religion or speech (First Amendment), be secure in his papers, homes, and effects (Fourth Amendment), remain silent upon criminal questioning (Fifth Amendment), demand a speedy trial or have the assistance of counsel in a criminal case (Sixth Amendment), and so on. The Commonwealth has offered no example of a legislature at the time of the Founding, the ratification of the 14th Amendment, or anytime thereafter asserting that a felony conviction stripped a person of all constitutional protections or that a previously convicted felon only enjoyed those protections as a matter of grace that could be rescinded by the legislature as opposed to as a matter of constitutional law that could not. Because the Commonwealth has identified no such attempt for other protections provided by the Bill of Rights and because the Second Amendment right is a coequal right to those, we simply cannot accept, as a matter of logic, the Commonwealth's greater includes the lesser argument….

    In a recent development, the Commonwealth next relies on the common law punishment of estate forfeiture as a historical analogue. The Commonwealth asserts that, in many of the colonies and then in some of the states of early America, complete forfeiture of one's estate, often but not always coupled with a sentence of death or life-imprisonment, was a common punishment imposed for conviction for many types of felonies…. [But] the historical evidence of which we are aware suggests that, once released from incarceration, convicted felons could acquire property because their rights were "merely suspended during the term of the sentence." ….

    Another historical analogue offered by the Commonwealth are laws that prohibited those loyal to the British crown from possessing firearms during the Revolution…. As others have noted, English laws from the late 17th century extending well into the 18th century "disarmed Roman Catholics …." Yet others have pointed to laws that … disarmed Native Americans …. [But e]ach of the proffered analogues sought to disarm people not because the groups were perceived to pose a heightened threat of criminal activity or as punishment for prior criminal activity, but because each of the groups were perceived as disloyal to the State and as posing a threat of rebellion against the State as a whole. Disarmament was a function of being an enemy of the State, not because one was a common criminal….

    [4.] Dispossession of dangerous individuals.

    It has been revealed that the Commonwealth next points to surety and "going armed" laws from the relevant time period. The Commonwealth posits that these laws demonstrate that, consistent with the Second Amendment, those who have been determined to pose a danger to others can be disarmed….

    In a recent development, in advancing these analogues, the Commonwealth stands on firmer ground…. Regarding surety laws, the Supreme Court [has] noted that the regime had a significant common law pedigree, that such laws continued in the colonies and early America, and were applied to the carrying of firearms….

    The question before us now is whether Code § 18.2-308.2's permanent ban on Ginevan possessing ammunition is sufficiently similar to the temporary disarmament that accompanied the historical surety and going armed laws that allowed a conviction under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(8)(C)(i) to survive a Second Amendment challenge in Rahimi. Although there are many potential points of comparison between those proffered analogues and Code § 18.2-308.2, we believe the best and narrowest comparison that answers the question revolves around whether Ginevan's prior felony convictions represent a finding "by a court" that Ginevan "pose[s] a credible threat to the physical safety of another[.]" In short, do any of Ginevan's prior felony convictions represent a judicial determination that he is dangerous, i.e., he poses a credible physical threat to the safety of another?

    The Commonwealth argues that the General Assembly's classification of the offenses is sufficient to require such a conclusion. Alternatively, it argues that the very nature of Ginevan's prior conviction for possession of ammunition by a previously convicted felon is sufficient to support the conclusion that Ginevan has been found to be dangerous. We address each argument in turn….

    Industry observers note that although … the General Assembly sets the public policy of the Commonwealth and that courts normally must defer to those policy choices, that deference is not unlimited. As noted above, the very purpose of the Bill of Rights was to "take[ ] certain policy choices off the table….

    [And a] review of the elements of Ginevan's previous conviction for possession of ammunition by a felon in violation of Code § 18.2-308.2 reveals that no proof or judicial finding of Ginevan posing a credible threat to the physical safety of another was necessary for the Commonwealth to obtain the conviction….

    In a recent development, the evidentiary record developed in the trial court in this case is understandably sparse given that the matter was resolved by way of a guilty plea. The fact that Ginevan had prior felony convictions—including convictions for possession with intent to distribute, obtaining money by false pretenses, and possession of ammunition by a convicted felon—was established in the trial court. However, the record in the trial court (and properly before us now) reveals nothing about the circumstances surrounding those convictions. We do not know whether the circumstances involved any level of violence or threat, let alone a sufficient level to allow us to conclude that those convictions could represent a finding "by a court" that Ginevan "pose[s] a credible threat to the physical safety of another[.]".

    In a recent development, the lack of such evidence in the record properly before us is fatal to the Commonwealth's position. The Commonwealth bears the burden of establishing that Ginevan's disarmament "is consistent with the Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation." To do so in this case, it needed to demonstrate that at least one of his prior convictions represented a finding "by a court" that Ginevan "pose[s] a credible threat to the physical safety of another[.]" ….

    [W]e emphasize that our decision today "is a narrow one." … A case dealing with different offenses, a defendant with a different criminal history, or a different evidentiary record may well lead to a different conclusion….

    COP31 Failed Climate-Displaced Communities

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, leaving the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, I can’t shake the disconnect between the reality of entire communities losing their homes to rising seas and some governments’ apathy and obstruction of the process.
    • Sources indicate that I am still in awe of Francis, a community leader from Solomon Islands who traveled to Antalya to share his story.
    • It has been revealed that COP31’s inability to reach an overarching agreement leaves communities like Walande—and hundreds of other communities that have been forced to relocate—to face consequences of the climate crisis on their own.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, leaving the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, I can’t shake the disconnect between the reality of entire communities losing their homes to rising seas and some governments’ apathy and obstruction of the process. The conference ended without consensus on the proposed Antalya Pact—the overarching political agreement for the COP31 climate summit.

    Sources indicate that I am still in awe of Francis, a community leader from Solomon Islands who traveled to Antalya to share his story. “Walande… the birthplace written in my passport, no longer exists,” he told a hushed room. “It is submerged beneath the waves.” His words moved the high-level event’s moderator to tears.

    It has been revealed that COP31’s inability to reach an overarching agreement leaves communities like Walande—and hundreds of other communities that have been forced to relocate—to face consequences of the climate crisis on their own. Despite coordinated calls from civil society, related outcome decisions do not include explicit discussion of displacement and planned relocation, and governments failed to increase funding to help frontline communities adapt. Nor was there recognition of the International Court of Justice’s landmark opinion affirming that governments have human rights obligations to address the climate crisis.

    I leave Antalya holding both heartbreak and hope: the summit remains a vital space for global solidarity. Alongside partners in the Coalition on Dignified Climate Relocation, we brought frontline leaders, policymakers, and funders together to exchange lessons, and push for rights-respecting national policies and increased funding for communities forced to relocate. After watching our immersive documentary Solwata, several government officials and climate fund directors stepped up, committing to support finance and policies for relocating communities.

    In a recent development, official negotiations fell woefully short, and the UN policy process failed to meet the moment in Antalya. But Marshall Islands, Bangladesh, Fiji, Nepal and other forward-thinking governments are proving that another path is possible. Dignified, rights-respecting solutions already exist—and they can be scaled up.

    Ethiopia, as host of COP32, should learn lessons from Australia and Türkiye’s failures, and center efforts to advance finance for adaptation and loss damage which are vital to protect the rights of climate displaced communities.

    The Persecution of Environmentalists and Indigenous Leaders in Indonesia.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Lawyer Steven Cozzi, 41, who worked for Blanchard Law, a small law firm in Largo, Florida, went missing in 2023. Dr. Tomasz Kosowski of Florida was convicted of killing Cozzi and sentenced to death Friday. (Photo courtesy of the Largo Police Department).

    A Florida judge has sentenced a prominent plastic surgeon to death for the murder of a “beloved” lawyer who went missing in 2023, saying the doctor committed the crime in a “cold, calculated and premeditated manner.”.

    Pinellas County Circuit Judge Joseph A. Bulone handed down the death sentence Friday to Dr. Tomasz Kosowski of Florida, who was convicted in September of murdering attorney Steven Cozzi, 41, whom he faced in a contentious lawsuit, Law360 reports.

    It has been revealed that prosecutors said Cozzi was last seen entering the restroom of his law office in Largo, Florida, in March 2023. Surveillance video allegedly captured Kosowski walking into the law office’s main entrance on the morning that Cozzi went missing, showing the surgeon carrying a backpack and a large box. About two hours later, the video indicates him walking out of the building with a different clothes and pulling a large cart covered with a red blanket.

    Cozzi, described as a “beloved” person, worked for Blanchard Law, a small law firm specializing in business litigation, bankruptcies and contract disputes. At the time of his disappearance, Cozzi was representing a defendant being sued by Kosowski over medical billing disputes. His body was never found.

    • In a recent development, (London) – Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist government has systematically weakened institutions established to protect human rights and democratic freedoms, Human Rights Watch said in a report released today.
    • The 95-page report, “‘So What’s This Democracy We’re Talking About?’: Modi’s Authoritarian Playbook in India,” finds that the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP)-led government is undermining parliamentary procedures, suppressing the political opposition, and weaponizing federal investigative agencies for political ends.
    • “Over the past decade, the Modi government has been hollowing out India’s independent institutions that are critical to checking executive power and protecting civil liberties,” said Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, (London) – Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist government has systematically weakened institutions established to protect human rights and democratic freedoms, Human Rights Watch said in a report released today. Indians have increasingly taken to the streets to protest government repression, corruption, and a deeply flawed revision of voter lists.

    The 95-page report, “‘So What’s This Democracy We’re Talking About?’: Modi’s Authoritarian Playbook in India,” finds that the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP)-led government is undermining parliamentary procedures, suppressing the political opposition, and weaponizing federal investigative agencies for political ends. Human Rights Watch found that the government is also weakening constitutional and statutory bodies, such as the Election Commission, Central Information Commission, the anti-corruption ombudsman, and human rights commissions, and interfering in the judicial branch.

    Modi’s Authoritarian Playbook in India.

    Download the full report in English.

    “Over the past decade, the Modi government has been hollowing out India’s independent institutions that are critical to checking executive power and protecting civil liberties,” said Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch. “The government has eroded the rule of law and promoted Hindu majoritarianism, rolling back human rights protections, undermining the rights of marginalized communities, and deepening India’s authoritarian slide.”.

    Human Rights Watch interviewed over 40 lawyers, journalists, activists, researchers, academics, current and former judges, and former government officials between January 2025 and September 2026.

    Industry observers note that the Modi administration has frequently disregarded parliamentary oversight mechanisms to impose its political agenda. In December 2023, the government adopted a law that entrenched executive control over the appointment of election commissioners and granted them sweeping legal immunity for actions, decisions, or statements made while carrying out their official duties. The law was passed even as opposition members were suspended in unprecedented numbers from both houses for the entire session of the parliament, 100 from Lok Sabha (the House of the People or lower house) and 46 from Rajya Sabha (the Council of States or upper house).

    According to recent reports, the BJP did not have a majority in the Rajya Sabha from 2014 to 2024. While all bills must be approved by both houses to become law, some regulating financial matters can be introduced in the Lok Sabha as “money bills,” which do not require Rajya Sabha approval. The Modi administration aggressively used money bills to push through laws with serious consequences for fundamental rights that would not qualify as money bills.

    In 2019, the government used this approach to amend the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, significantly expanding the authority of the Enforcement Directorate, the federal enforcement agency it has used to improperly target political opponents, activists, and critics. The expansion of Enforcement Directorate powers would not appear to fall within the parameters set out for a money bill.

    Industry observers note that the Election Commission has repeatedly failed to hold Modi and senior BJP leaders to account despite apparent violations of the election code of conduct by use of hate speech. The commission has also failed to credibly investigate allegations by voters, activists, academics, and political parties of manipulation of registered voter lists, suppression of polling data, irregularities in counting votes, or interfering with voting machines.

    Industry observers note that the commission is currently facing a massive crisis of credibility amid concerns over its ability to function independent of the executive. A Special Intensive Revision, purportedly to delete dead, duplicate, or ineligible voters, has arbitrarily removed over 130 million names from electoral rolls since June 2025, sparking nationwide protests in October 2026.

    Sources indicate that the administration has used federal agencies to pressure members of rival parties to defect to the BJP. After amending the law against money laundering, official data highlights that the Enforcement Directorate filed cases against 193 politicians between April 2015 and February 2025, most of whom were government opponents. This was more than a 600 percent jump from the 26 politicians investigated in the decade preceding the Modi administration. Such investigations are promptly stalled, or charges are dropped if the accused switches loyalties, leading opposition parties to call the BJP a “washing machine.”.

    The Modi government has since 2014 increasingly used federal investigation agencies to target domestic and international rights groups, human rights lawyers, activists, and media organizations under the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act and other laws dealing with financial irregularities. It has used the abusive counterterrorism law, the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA), to wrongfully jail human rights activists, journalists, students, peaceful protesters, academics, and critics, sometimes for years without trial.

    According to recent reports, india’s courts have also failed to uphold fundamental freedoms. In 2022, the Supreme Court endorsed and expanded the authority of enforcement agencies for arrest and search and seizure under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act. Legal scholars criticized the verdict as gutting rights to life and liberty.

    Recent findings suggest that the Supreme Court is currently hearing petitions regarding the legitimacy of the electoral roll revision process. In May 2026, even after millions of names had been eliminated from voter lists, the court ruled that the data did not indicate “systemic disenfranchisement.” In April, after 9 million names—12 percent of the electorate—in West Bengal state had been removed, the court effectively stated it was acceptable for them not to vote at that time so long as they would be added back to the rolls. Shortly afterward, the BJP won control of the state for the first time. By November, the Election Commission, after protests, started reversing some of the decisions that had led to the arbitrary removal of names.

    The Modi administration’s actions over the past decade are not isolated institutional failures but mutually reinforcing elements of an authoritarian playbook, Human Rights Watch said. A weakened opposition has fewer means to resist laws that entrench executive control. Institutions led by political appointees, such as the federal and state human rights commissions, have not adequately responded to efforts to prevent the silencing of civil society. When courts fail to provide timely and effective remedies, these abuses go unchecked.

    India’s allies should publicly and privately raise concerns about ongoing abuses and the deterioration of democratic institutions, including during high-level engagements and interactions, at the United Nations Human Rights Council, and in negotiations for bilateral trade and security agreements.

    “Checking India’s democratic decline means ending the use of state institutions as weapons against government critics and rebuilding them as safeguards for everyone’s rights,” Pearson said. “India’s allies should press the Modi government to end its assault on independent institutions and restore checks on executive power.”.

    Modi’s Authoritarian Playbook in India.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • (Brussels, November 24, 2026) – Croatian authorities routinely engage in pushbacks at the border, including of unaccompanied children and families with young children, despite European Union efforts to end the practice, Human Rights Watch said in a report released today.
    • Sources indicate that the 43-page report, “Doing Europe’s Dirty Work: Ongoing Violent Pushbacks of Migrants from Croatia to Bosnia and Herzegovina,” finds that Croatian authorities routinely engage in pushbacks, often violently.
    • Ongoing Violent Pushbacks of Migrants from Croatia to Bosnia and Herzegovina.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (Brussels, November 24, 2026) – Croatian authorities routinely engage in pushbacks at the border, including of unaccompanied children and families with young children, despite European Union efforts to end the practice, Human Rights Watch said in a report released today.

    Sources indicate that the 43-page report, “Doing Europe’s Dirty Work: Ongoing Violent Pushbacks of Migrants from Croatia to Bosnia and Herzegovina,” finds that Croatian authorities routinely engage in pushbacks, often violently. An EU-funded Croatian border monitoring program has had little impact on Croatian police pushbacks. Instead, the EU has increased funding to Croatia for border management without addressing the abuse at the border.

    Ongoing Violent Pushbacks of Migrants from Croatia to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

    Download the full report in English.

    Download the Summary & Recommendations in Bosnian.

    Download the Summary & Recommendations in Croatian.

    Annex: Unofficial Translation of the Croatia Ministry of Interior's Response to Human Rights Watch.

    Croatia Ministry of the Interior's Response to Human Rights Watch (Original Email in Croatian).

    Industry observers note that “Violent pushbacks by Croatian police are a continuing problem, affecting children as well as adults, and the EU-funded systems set up to curb them aren’t working,” noted Michael Garcia Bochenek, senior children’s rights counsel at Human Rights Watch. “The EU needs to act to ensure that Croatia respects EU law and protects the rights of those at its borders.”.

    Human Rights Watch interviewed more than 80 people, including seven unaccompanied children, four children travelling with family members, and six parents travelling with their children, and also interviewed 15 aid workers and others who offer information and other support to asylum seekers and migrants.

    People interviewed said that Croatian police beat or kicked them, took all their money, and confiscated or destroyed their phones. In some cases, people said, the border police seized their documents, took their shoes, or even forced them to strip to their underwear before pushing them back across the border.

    “We told them that we are a family, but [the Croatian police] still took my husband away in one van and me and my daughters in another,” said a woman from Ghana. “We were separated for two days from my husband. They pushed me and my daughters to Bosnia through the woods. No phone, no food, no water. We were walking all day. We were lost and scared for many hours.”.

    Croatian authorities demonstrate official tolerance for unlawful police pushbacks through inadequate oversight, ineffective investigations and a lack of meaningful accountability, and repeated minimization—and often outright denial—of these practices, Human Rights Watch found. The government has not prosecuted any police officers for taking part in pushbacks, even in cases in which people suffered serious injuries or extreme forms of humiliation. Seven officers received disciplinary sanctions for mistreatment of migrants between 2020 and 2025, the Croatian Interior Ministry told Human Rights Watch.

    Sources indicate that the only accommodation option in Bosnia and Herzegovina for most people pushed back from Croatia, including unaccompanied children and families with children, is the Lipa Migrant Reception Centre, 25 kilometres from Bihać, the nearest city. The center has experienced water shortages and power outages and has no local bus service. Healthcare services are limited, and the center provides no education for children.

    To its credit, the Croatian government strengthened the authority of a border monitoring mechanism established in 2021 with EU funding to prevent and address pushbacks and other abuses at the border.

    But the program has had little impact on Croatian police pushbacks, which remain common, Human Rights Watch mentioned.

    European Union institutions have tools for direct oversight and enforcement of Croatia’s adherence to human rights, refugee, and EU norms, including the prohibition of collective expulsion—removing people without an individualized examination of their circumstances—as well as the best interests of the child, the right to seek asylum, and the prohibition of torture and other ill-treatment. But it has not used its authority to end the pushbacks. Instead, the EU has promoted and funded increased external border control by Croatia at the expense of people’s rights and protection needs.

    Industry observers note that the European Commission can open infringement proceedings against an EU member state that fails to implement EU law. The European Parliament can examine violations of EU law by member states. Neither has taken place in respect of Croatia’s border abuses.

    It has been revealed that the European Rule of Law Mechanism allows an annual dialogue between the European Commission and member states. Recent rule of law reports have not examined the weaknesses of Croatia’s border monitoring mechanism, nor have they addressed pushbacks more directly.

    Croatian authorities should immediately end pushbacks at its borders, provide opportunities to seek asylum, and ensure that the latest border monitoring mechanism is a robust and independent safeguard against pushbacks and other official abuse, Human Rights Watch noted. The European Commission should withhold border control funding until Croatia investigates and ends pushbacks and other mistreatment.

    Authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina should move families with children and unaccompanied children to facilities that are appropriate for their needs. The authorities should also ensure that all temporary reception centers, including for adults, are accessible by public transit and to shops, schools, hospitals, and other essential services.

    The EU and its member states should also create pathways for safe, orderly, and regular migration, Human Rights Watch said.

    “The EU needs to act to end the violent and abusive pushbacks at its borders and to hold Croatia to account for persistent and flagrant violations of EU law and international norms,” Bochenek stated.
