    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that A federal jury in the Eastern District of New York returned guilty verdicts following a three-month trial against Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd. (Huawei) and three of its subsidiaries for violating U.S. sanctions involving Iran, lying to banks, money laundering, and stealing trade secrets from American companies. As proven at trial, Huawei and several of its subsidiaries, including Chinese subsidiary Huawei Device Co. Ltd. (Huawei Device) and U.S. subsidiaries Futurewei Technologies Inc. (Futurewei) and Huawei Device USA Inc. (Huawei Device USA), engaged in a decades-long scheme to enrich Huawei and grow its telecommunications business, including in the United States, through criminal activities.

    Recent findings suggest that “No person or company is above the law,” stated Attorney General Todd Blanche. “For decades, Huawei and three of its subsidiaries conducted their business in the United States on the basis of lies and theft. Thanks to the work of the FBI and our federal prosecutors, those who engaged in these criminal activities will be held accountable.”.

    Recent findings suggest that “For over two decades, Huawei built its global empire on a foundation of fraud, theft, and deception,” said Assistant Attorney General Tysen A. Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “Huawei’s crimes threatened the U.S. financial system, took advantage of American companies that compete honestly in the global telecommunications market, and undermined our national security. Today’s verdict sends an unmistakable message: America will defend its businesses, protect its workers, and safeguard its national security against corrupt foreign corporations that lie, cheat, and steal to get ahead.”.

    Industry observers note that “Huawei violated our laws, empowered our enemies, and harmed our national security,” remarked Acting Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M. Scott Proctor. “This conviction reveals that the National Security Division and its partners will not rest until companies like Huawei are held to account for their bad conduct in an American court of justice.”.

    “Few crimes are as serious as Huawei’s decades-long pattern of endangering U.S. national security, violating the sanctity of U.S. commerce, and impeding the enforcement of U.S. laws,” said U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. for the Eastern District of New York. “Today’s verdict is a step towards accountability for Huawei’s criminal activities, which includes yearslong collaboration with sanctioned entities in Iran, repeated lies to banks, and blatant thefts from U.S. technology companies.”.

    Sources indicate that “For years, Huawei and its subsidiaries carried out an egregious campaign to expand their international enterprise through theft of trade secrets, fraud, and other criminal conduct at the expense of U.S. companies and the rule of law,” said Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division. “This case serves as a stark reminder that the Chinese government continues to pose a serious threat to our economic and national security, but today’s guilty verdict proves the FBI and our partners will aggressively investigate, expose, and hold accountable those who target our nation. No company is too significant, too powerful, or too well connected to exploit the U.S. and its citizens and expect to escape American justice.”.

    Huawei and its subsidiaries assisted the government of the Islamic Republic of Iran by providing turnkey services with respect to an internet backbone and broader accessibility for mobile networks in the country. Huawei also helped the Iranian regime and a component of the Iranian intelligence apparatus, Zaeim, to monitor and censor its users’ access to the internet. Testimony further established that Huawei provided surveillance cameras that enabled the Iranian regime to monitor protest activity.

    Huawei conducted its business in Iran under the name “Skycom.” Huawei repeatedly lied about the nature of its business in Iran, falsely telling banks, journalists, and the U.S. government that it did not assist Iran’s government, military, or intelligence community; that it began restricting its business in Iran in 2011; that Skycom was a business partner, rather than a wholly-owned subsidiary; and that Huawei complied with all applicable sanctions. Huawei knew that all of those statements were materially false and misleading.

    It has been revealed that huawei lied about its activities in Iran to banks to obtain billions of U.S. dollars and access to U.S.-dollar clearing services, which enabled Huawei to be a sophisticated participant in a global marketplace for telecommunications services — in part because of its lies.

    The jury convicted Huawei and three subsidiaries of conspiracy to steal trade secrets, conspiracy to commit wire and bank fraud, wire fraud, bank fraud, conspiracy to defraud the United States, conspiracy to violate the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), substantive violations of IEEPA, and money laundering conspiracy. When sentenced, the defendants face financial penalties including criminal fines, forfeiture, and restitution. Sentencing has been set for Sept. 14, 2027. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.

    The investigation is being conducted by the FBI’s Latest York Field Office.

    Trial Attorneys Taylor G. Stout, Morgan Cohen, and Jasmin Salehi Fashemi of the Criminal Division’s Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section (MNF), Trial Attorney Aaron L. Jennen of the National Security Division’s Counterintelligence and Export Control Section, and Assistant U.S. Attorneys Alexander A. Solomon, Meredith A. Arfa, Robert M. Pollack, Matthew Skurnik, and Matthew F. Sullivan for the Eastern District of Upcoming York (EDNY) are prosecuting the case, with assistance provided by Assistant U.S. Attorney Brendan G. King, EDNY paralegal specialists Matthew Jennings and Grace Yang, and MNF paralegal specialists Christina Roman, Alexa Stiles, Heather DePremio, Jackson Mayo, and Angela R. Ancalle Jiménez.

    MNF’s mission is to take the profit out of crime, eliminate drug cartels, and protect the U.S. financial system. MNF pursues criminal prosecutions and criminal and civil asset recovery actions involving: financial facilitators who launder profits for criminals; financial institutions and their officers and employees whose actions threaten the U.S. financial system and financial institutions; international money launderers who support transnational organized crime; and the top command and control of international drug trafficking organizations.

    MNF’s Bank Integrity Unit investigates and prosecutes banks and other financial institutions, including their officers, managers and employees whose actions threaten the integrity of the individual institution or the wider financial system.

    #124401. The Supreme Court before it stood apart

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1590 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    The Supreme Court before it stood apart

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1590 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that the Political Supreme Court: A Forgotten History by Rachel A.
    • In her excellent new book, The Political Supreme Court: A Forgotten History, professor Rachel Shelden closes with Chief Justice John Roberts’ insistence that “you don’t want the political branches telling you what the law is,” and that public opinion should not guide the court’s decisions.
    • Sources indicate that that will likely sound quite familiar: it is how we have come to think about the Supreme Court.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that the Political Supreme Court: A Forgotten History by Rachel A. Shelden (The University of North Carolina Press).

    In her excellent new book, The Political Supreme Court: A Forgotten History, professor Rachel Shelden closes with Chief Justice John Roberts’ insistence that “you don’t want the political branches telling you what the law is,” and that public opinion should not guide the court’s decisions.

    Sources indicate that that will likely sound quite familiar: it is how we have come to think about the Supreme Court. But Shelden’s history demonstrates that the 19th century court and the way Americans perceived it were very different. Indeed, the modern idea of the detached judge, the justice as apolitical “umpire,” is not nearly as originalist as we tend to assume.

    It has been revealed that shelden opens with Abraham Lincoln arguing before the court in 1849. The court that Lincoln and his fellow members of the bar knew was not the marble institution, removed from ordinary political life, that we picture today. For example, the justices “rode circuit.” Each was assigned a region, generally the part of the country from which he hailed and in which he traveled through to preside over federal trial courts. This brought the justices into regular contact with local lawyers, officials, and communities.

    Shelden calls this “judicial representation”: the idea that a justice would bring a region’s perspective to the court because he knew the people he impliedly represented. Although today’s justices are assigned to a circuit, typically the circuit to which they have ties geographically, the concept is now decidedly different; except at certain prescheduled events, justices no longer directly communicate with the people in that circuit as part of their duties, but handle applications from it in the corridors of the marble palace. “Judicial representation” is most definitely no longer a thing.

    It has been revealed that but this just scratches the surface of the differences that Shelden lays out. In the 19th century, the justices were active participants in the political debates of their time, in ways that today would not only be grounds for profound criticism but even potential impeachment.

    Chief Justice John Marshall was himself an active participant in such discourse. In 1800, before becoming chief, Marshall began contributing to the Washington Federalist, a newspaper established to support President John Adams and later oppose Thomas Jefferson. Marshall’s involvement was so extensive that he became known as the brains behind the paper. Nor did his appointment to the court entirely sever his connection to it. Elias Caldwell, the Supreme Court’s clerk during Marshall’s tenure, subsequently became its proprietor. The paper remained staunchly Federalist under Caldwell’s leadership, regularly attacking the Jefferson administration’s policies as unconstitutional.

    Marshall’s political opponents suspected that he continued to exert considerable influence behind the scenes at the Washington Federalist even as chief justice, directing those attacks. Indeed, the Philadelphia Aurora, a newspaper aligned with Jefferson, described Caldwell as “a creature of John Marshall, chief justice.” Shelden casts doubt on Caldwell’s denial of Marshall’s involvement. And given that Caldwell was Marshall’s own clerk at the Supreme Court, you can understand the skepticism.

    Justice William Johnson provides another example. In 1823, Johnson ruled (in his lower-court circuit-riding role) that South Carolina’s Negro Seamen Act, which authorized the detention of free Black sailors arriving in Charleston, violated the Constitution. Local officials were furious and refused to publish his opinion in the newspapers. So Johnson took his argument directly to the public, putting his opinion in a pamphlet that was circulated around the country, and then supporting the decision via pseudonymously authored op-eds that submitted his interpretation of the Constitution was correct.

    According to recent reports, nor were the justices’ newspaper writings limited to defending their decisions. In 1848, Justice John McLean published letters addressing such political issues as the national bank, taxation, infrastructure, and the Mexican-American War, all while his supporters were encouraging him to pursue the presidency.

    And in 1859, Justice John Catron publicly opposed proposed Tennessee legislation that would have enslaved free Black residents who remained in the state. Catron used his connections at the Nashville Union and American to publish a letter criticizing the legislation. The newspaper’s editors attacked his position, producing a public back-and-forth in its pages. Catron’s letter was even reprinted in Missouri, where similar legislation was under consideration. Tennessee ultimately rejected the proposal, and Shelden suggests Catron’s intervention may have mattered.

    To put this in perspective, such actions would be akin to Justice Clarence Thomas writing an opinion piece in The Wall Street Journal defending the Republican Party’s position on disputed legislation, or Justice Elena Kagan publishing an article in The Latest York Times supporting a Democratic president’s legislative agenda.

    Yet the justices’ political involvement went well beyond expressing opinions publicly. Some actually ran for elected office while continuing to serve on the court.

    Shelden recounts the example of Justice Smith Thompson, who accepted the nomination for governor of Upcoming York in 1828 while a justice. Thompson ultimately lost to Martin Van Buren by more than 30,000 votes. After losing the election, Thompson simply continued serving on the court, where he remained for another 15 years.

    It has been revealed that justice McLean, meanwhile, was discussed as a potential presidential candidate in the 1830s, with political allies contemplating his nomination even as he continued hearing cases. Indeed, both McLean and his colleague, Justice Levi Woodbury, would later emerge as presidential contenders in 1848.

    In a recent development, justice William Johnson, appointed by President Thomas Jefferson, actually won election as a commissioner of the poor in Charleston Neck, South Carolina, in 1826. In this role, he exercised authority over local taxation, patronage, and public resources. Johnson held this elected position, and won reelection, while continuing to serve on the Supreme Court.

    Again, by way of comparison, imagine Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson declaring herself a candidate for the 2028 presidential election – while continuing to decide cases and write opinions. Or contemplate Justice Neil Gorsuch simultaneously holding an elected local government office with taxing authority.

    Recent findings suggest that just as notable was the willingness of justices to involve themselves directly in the work of the other branches of government. In doing so, they corresponded with presidents and members of Congress about public policy. They even offered advice on legislation and, in some instances, helped craft it.

    Recent findings suggest that during Reconstruction, Chief Justice Salmon Chase pressed President Andrew Johnson on Black suffrage and used his political relationships to influence Reconstruction policy. For his part, just a few years earlier, Justice John Campbell of Alabama sought to influence President-elect Lincoln to problem a public statement reassuring Southern moderates that his administration would not interfere with slavery in their states. Campbell even offered to publish a letter in his own name, as a citizen of Alabama, to help create an occasion for Lincoln to make such a statement.

    It has been revealed that when Lincoln declined to act, Campbell turned to President James Buchanan. He urged Buchanan to send commissioners to the secession conventions to persuade the delegates to preserve the Union. Campbell’s efforts ultimately failed. But consider what he was doing: a sitting Supreme Court justice was privately advising both an incoming and an outgoing president about how to address the most consequential political crisis in the nation’s history.

    Now imagine Chief Justice John Roberts privately consulting with President Donald Trump about birthright citizenship, or Justice Sonia Sotomayor advising former President Joe Biden about his unconstitutional student loan forgiveness program and how it could be fixed.

    In the dénouement of the book, Shelden traces how the political world of the justices changed as the 19th century drew to a close. Circuit riding ended, the legal profession grew more formal, and the court became more centered in Washington. As the country marked the Constitution’s centennial, lawyers and judges helped tell a newly introduced story of the court, one that made political detachment seem like some sort of longstanding tradition. (To be fair, this did not bring such political involvement to an immediate end.).

    If I have one criticism of Shelden’s otherwise excellent work, it is that she doesn’t explore this transformation in nearly the same depth as she does the earlier history. How, exactly, did the justices (and their fellow Americans) come to accept a view of the court so different from the one they had held for much of the 19th century, and which we hold today? That is a fascinating question in its own right, and perhaps the worthy subject of a follow-up volume.

    Regardless, Shelden’s history offers a challenge to today’s justices, as well as to proponents and critics of the modern court. Nineteenth-century justices participated much more freely in political life, while today’s justices insist that they must stand apart from politics, even as many Americans cast a dubious side eye upon that claim. Was it better when justices did not deny the political world they inhabited and were a part of? And can the way we look at the court, and the way the justices see themselves, change again? I don’t think the answers are obvious. But Shelden’s book made clear to me that a reflexive dismissal of such questions is based more on historical ignorance than any fixed tradition of the Supreme Court as appearing apolitical.

    Mark Miller directs Environment and Natural Resources litigation at Pacific Legal Foundation.

    According to recent reports, recommended Citation: Mark Miller, The Supreme Court before it stood apart, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 18, 2026, 10:00 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/the-supreme-court-before-it-stood-apart/.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 24, 2026, 11:32 am CST.

    Recent findings suggest that A Washington superior court judge received an admonishment Friday from the Washington Commission on Judicial Conduct for commenting on “violence from the Native American community,” causing courtroom onlookers to react in shock and offense. (Image from Shutterstock).

    A Washington superior court judge received an admonishment Friday from the Washington Commission on Judicial Conduct for commenting on “violence from the Native American community,” causing courtroom onlookers to react in shock and offense.

    Recent findings suggest that mason County Superior Court Judge Monty D. Cobb made the remark while sentencing a defendant who pleaded guilty to killing a fellow member of the Skokomish Tribe.

    Cobb said it was “extremely unfortunate that I see way too many acts of violence from the Native community,” according to coverage by Law360.

    Many tribal members were inside the courtroom when Cobb made the statement, and two complaints reported to the Washington Commission on Judicial Conduct prompted a confidential investigation.

    The investigation “determined that the quoted comments caused shock and offense among the onlookers and a sense that respondent was blaming the community for its experience of high rates of violence,” the judicial conduct commission’s report said.

    Cobb admitted to violating two rules: Canon 1, Rules 1.1 and 1.2 of the Washington Code of Judicial Conduct, which requires judges to conduct themselves in a manner that promotes public confidence in the judiciary’s integrity and impartiality and to avoid the appearance of impropriety.

    Recent findings suggest that the judge’s sanction, in part, includes reading the state’s Code of Judicial Conduct “in its entirety” and confirming in writing. The investigation’s document noted that courtroom observers think that Cobb “does not harbor a bias against Indigenous people or other marginalized groups, and that everyone is treated fairly in his courtroom.”.

    Justice Department Confirms Largest-Ever Crackdown on Scammers, Targeting Over 800 Defendants to Protect Americans from Fraud

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2748 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fbi

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that today, the Justice Department confirmed the results of a historic surge in resources to protect Americans from criminal scam networks and online fraud following President Trump’s Executive Order 14390 directing a government-wide crackdown.
    • In a recent development, these actions include new charges, extraditions, guilty verdicts, and criminal sentences.
    • Recent findings suggest that “Predatory scams against the American people will not be tolerated,” stated Attorney General Todd Blanche.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that today, the Justice Department confirmed the results of a historic surge in resources to protect Americans from criminal scam networks and online fraud following President Trump’s Executive Order 14390 directing a government-wide crackdown. Since the Executive Order was signed on March 6, Justice Department prosecutors have taken action to protect Americans in over 400 cases against over 800 defendants.

    In a recent development, these actions include new charges, extraditions, guilty verdicts, and criminal sentences. U.S. prosecutors and agents also assisted law enforcement in over 10 countries in raids of foreign scam call centers and compounds that targeted Americans.

    Recent findings suggest that “Predatory scams against the American people will not be tolerated,” stated Attorney General Todd Blanche. “The unprecedented results of this surge are just the beginning. We will continue prosecuting those who perpetrate these schemes and disrupting the activities of transnational criminal organizations before they reach American shores.”.

    “Under President Trump’s Executive Order 14390, this FBI has made dismantling predatory scam enterprises a top priority using a whole-of-government approach,” said FBI Director Kash Patel. “Through Operation Blackout, this FBI’s scam center demolition initiative, we’ve seized nearly $17 billion in illicit funds, taken more than 14,000 digital devices, directly warned over 11,000 Americans from scam attempts, and prevented more than $690 million in potential victim losses. The Trump Administration is crushing scam centers plaguing Americans, and with Attorney General Blanche and our interagency partners, we are delivering on this righteous mission every day all over the world. The message to these scam syndicates is clear: if you target Americans, justice will find you.”.

    “Scammers worldwide steal billions of dollars from Americans each year, profiting from lies and vulnerability,” mentioned Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “Under President Trump and Attorney General Blanche, the Criminal Division is taking the fight directly to the criminal networks that are stealing from Americans. We will not allow these scammers to hide behind their screens or escape justice by committing these crimes abroad. The Justice Department will use every tool at its disposal to disrupt predatory schemes, punish wrongdoers, and protect the American people.”.

    Industry observers note that according to Gallup, 10% of U.S. adults experienced a scam last year, either directly or through someone in their household. Nearly three in four scam victims experienced a negative effect on their mental health or well-being. Gallup also reports that Americans lost an estimated $68 billion to scams in 2025 alone. These scams include cryptocurrency investment scams, financially motivated sextortion, government imposter schemes, and other predatory schemes that collectively cost Americans billions of dollars, with many families losing their life savings.

    In one scam charged this month, current and former members of prison gangs in Georgia used contraband mobile phones to falsely tell victims that they missed jury duty and would be arrested if they failed to pay a “fine.” 14 individuals were charged in three indictments in federal and state courts for participation in these schemes, and another 17 defendants were charged in state court for a scheme to smuggle contraband mobile phones, often used to perpetrate fraud schemes and other crimes, into Georgia prisons. Websites that were used by inmates to commit jury duty imposter schemes were seized. Below are social media posts by Georgia prison inmates flaunting the proceeds of fraud schemes and contraband mobile phones used to contact victims.

    The anti-scam surge was coordinated by the Justice Department's Criminal Division, which brought together a dedicated team of prosecutors to identify scammers, disrupt their networks, and hold them accountable. This team includes experts across the Criminal Division’s sections, including the White Collar and Corporate Enforcement Section, Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section, Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section, Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section, Human Rights and Special Prosecutions Section, Office of Overseas Prosecutorial Development, Assistance and Training, and the Office of International Affairs.

    The whole-of-government approach includes initiatives by the FBI, State Department, Department of Homeland Security, including Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) and U.S. Secret Service, Treasury Department, U.S. Postal Inspection Service (USPIS), Federal Communications Commission, Federal Trade Commission (FTC), Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, and Internal Revenue Service (IRS).

    During the surge period from March 6 to present, Assistant U.S. Attorneys and Criminal Division trial attorneys contributed to the surge by obtaining wide-ranging results in 85 federal districts across the country. 30 defendants were extradited to face scam-related charges in U.S. courts. Information about each case is highlighted on this interactive map.

    In the month leading up to today’s announcement alone, the Criminal Division filed and unsealed charges against over 30 scam defendants. In addition to the jury duty scam described above, additional schemes alleged and charged in these cases include:.

    More details on each scheme and additional Criminal Division surge actions are provided here.

    The Justice Department coordinated with other agencies to launch a public education and messaging campaign informing consumers of the dangers of fraud, providing guidance on avoiding schemes, and encouraging Americans to use the upcoming holiday season to “Share Your Scam Story” with friends and relatives.

    Operation Blackout is the FBI’s global counter-scam demolition initiative. Through intelligence-driven operations and close collaboration with international law enforcement and government partners, the FBI has restrained nearly $17 billion in illicit funds, seized more than 14,000 digital devices, and helped identify, disrupt, and dismantle over 29 scam compounds operating across Asia, Africa, and the Middle East. These operations resulted in the federal charging of more than 50 scam actors, while FBI coordination and investigative support enabled foreign partners to arrest or detain more than 320 additional perpetrators overseas.

    In a recent development, working alongside international partners, the FBI also assisted in the liberation and repatriation of more than 2,200 trafficked workers forced to operate inside scam compounds. Since Executive Order 14390 on March 6th, Operation Level Up has prevented more than $143 million in victim losses, warned thousands of Americans they were being targeted by a scammer and frozen over $350 million in assets through FBI’s Recovery Asset Team.

    As part of this coordinated global effort, the State Department funds U.S. law enforcement advisors who train and mentor foreign investigators and prosecutors to work on U.S. cases. In Southeast Asia, advisors mentor and provide technical assistance to local law enforcement on scam investigations. To date, the State Department funded and supported U.S. and Southeast Asian law enforcement to facilitate the freezing of more than $1 billion in stolen cryptocurrency, the takedown of over 1.4 million fraudulent websites and accounts, numerous arrests, and several pending extraditions. State Department-funded forensic tools helped analyze more than 10,000 devices and hard drives in Thailand alone, allowing U.S. and Thai law enforcement to better understand the criminal networks and advance U.S. investigations.

    In Moldova, the State Department trained local prosecutors who oversaw the October arrests of three suspects in an online romance scheme that took $440,000 from American and European victims in a single month. Additionally, the State Department provided investigative training, protective equipment, and forensics software that enabled raids in October that resulted in the closure of five call centers and detained eight suspected coordinators who allegedly ran fake cryptocurrency trading platforms that defrauded investors.

    It has been revealed that "Too many Americans have suffered from cyber fraud, particularly from scam operations emanating from Southeast Asia, and expanding across South Asia, the Middle East, Africa, and the Pacific. But the true cost is not in dollars alone. Behind every statistic is a human story – a family bankrupted, a retiree left destitute, or a young person driven to suicide," remarked Deputy Assistant Secretary of State David Bedard. "We know the threat is evolving, and we are prepared to develop fresh tools and strategies to prevent scammers and other criminals from stealing from and harming Americans. Cyber-enabled fraud is proliferating around the world, so we must stay vigilant and build partnerships to combat it.".

    Homeland Security Investigations.

    In a recent development, since March 6, HSI offices nationwide executed more than 300 arrests, worked with the Justice Department to indict more than 100 defendants, and secured approximately 80 convictions and guilty pleas. HSI’s financial fraud investigations have also resulted in the seizure, restraint, freezing, or recovery of more than $120 million dollars in illicit proceeds, including funds held in bank and cryptocurrency accounts, cash, precious metals, vehicles, real property, and other assets. HSI works with domestic and international law enforcement partners, prosecutors, financial institutions, and private-sector stakeholders to identify and dismantle the criminal networks responsible, trace and recover illicit proceeds, and pursue the return of funds to victims when legally authorized.

    “HSI is committed to identifying and dismantling the criminal networks that perpetrate these crimes, wherever they operate, while tracing and seizing illicit proceeds and pursuing the return of funds to victims whenever legally authorized,” noted HSI Acting Executive Associate Director John A. Condon. “Through close coordination with our domestic and international law enforcement partners, prosecutors, financial institutions, and private-sector stakeholders, HSI will continue to hold these actors accountable and protect the American public from evolving financial threats.”.

    Recent findings suggest that during the surge period, Secret Service investigators have restrained more than $200 million in illicit funds, disrupted 1,780 domains operated by scammers, and recovered more than $119 million while investigating more than 1,540 business email compromise incidents. Secret Service-led cases included the identification of a cryptocurrency investment conspiracy operated from scam centers in Cambodia that targeted at least 174 U.S. victims. In October, a Chinese national was extradited from the Netherlands and arraigned in the Central District of California for his alleged role in that conspiracy.

    “While we are encouraged by the progress made to date, our investigators continue to lead dozens of cases involving transnational criminal networks targeting the American people,” mentioned U.S. Secret Service Director Sean Curran. “Today’s announcement demonstrates that scammers operating anywhere in the world can be identified and brought to justice. The Secret Service remains committed to its founding mission of investigating financial crimes and will continue to work with law enforcement partners in the United States and around the world to dismantle and disrupt these criminal networks.”.

    During the surge period, USPIS supported cases against dozens of defendants, including those who perpetrated jury duty imposter schemes described above, lottery and sweepstakes fraud, inheritance fraud, and fraud against Spanish-speaking Americans. Several of these cases involved prosecutions of list brokers who knowingly provided the names of elderly Americans to fraudsters operating abroad. USPIS also seized three internet domains linked to jury duty imposter schemes perpetrated by Georgia prison inmates. Traffic to all three web addresses was redirected to official government servers displaying a public seizure banner. This coordinated takedown effectively dismantled the operators’ digital infrastructure and prevented further public victimization. USPIS also partnered with the Justice Department to mail out over 4,800 unlicensed money transmitter letters since March, which has had an incredible impact on the rates of reducing recidivism for “money mules.”.

    According to recent reports, “Behind every scam is a person whose financial security, trust, and peace of mind have been threatened,” said Chief Inspector Gary Barksdale. “The Postal Inspection Service brings investigative expertise, nationwide reach, and a longstanding commitment to protecting consumers to this effort. Together with the Department of Justice and our partners, the USPIS is working to disrupt these criminal networks, pursue accountability, and prevent others from becoming victims.”.

    During the surge period, the FTC filed 16 actions challenging deceptive earnings claims, unfair payment processing practices, tech support scams, debt relief schemes, unauthorized billing practices, misleading claims about health products, health insurance frauds, government and business impersonations, and deceptive claims about sextortion assistance services. The FTC sent warning letters to a dozen websites advising them of their obligations to comply with the TAKE IT DOWN Act and to 25 companies that market or generate sales leads for healthcare prepares, putting them on notice about deceptive or unfair claims that likely violate laws enforced by the FTC. The FTC has continued to work with domain registrars and others to take down social media pages and 19 websites impersonating the FTC or FTC officials. Since April 2026, the FTC has connected more than 365 callers to the Justice Department’s National Elder Fraud Hotline and provided the hotline number to more than 7,100 online filers.

    According to recent reports, “The FTC has been on the front lines of tackling fraud for more than a century,” said FTC Chairman and Anti-Fraud Task Force Vice Chairman Andrew N. Ferguson. “Thanks to President Trump’s comprehensive, government-wide approach to stopping fraud, the Trump FTC has returned almost $3 billion to American consumers who have been harmed by fraud and deception. The Trump Administration’s message to the bad actors who lie, cheat and steal to defraud Americans out of their hard-earned money is clear: you are living on borrowed time. The FTC is proud to work alongside its federal partners to protect Americans from scammers, whether the crooks are here at home or abroad.”.

    Securities and Exchange Commission.

    Sources indicate that since March 2026, the SEC has filed enforcement actions against 39 entities for allegedly filing false Forms ADV to create the appearance of legitimate U.S. investment advisers and lure retail investors and charged multiple entities with fraud in connection with so-called investment confidence scams that feigned SEC compliance while misappropriating more than $15 million from investors through online platforms. In the last year, the SEC also charged three purported crypto asset trading platforms and four investment clubs with allegedly defrauding retail investors of more than $14 million through an online investment-confidence scam. The SEC charged BG Wealth Sharing Ltd and DSJ Exchange Pty Ltd with an alleged investment fraud scheme that raised more than $130 million from tens of thousands of retail investors across the U.S. and abroad. The SEC has issued investor alerts warning investors that fraudsters may use social media platforms and messaging apps or claim to be officially registered with the SEC to lure investors into scams. The SEC also encourages investors to visit Investor.gov to verify the background of individuals offering investment opportunities.

    “Advances in technology have lowered the barriers to entry for fraudsters, making it easier to reach potential victims and making fraudulent schemes appear more legitimate,” stated David Woodcock, Director of the SEC's Division of Enforcement. “The technology may be new, but the frauds are familiar. We will continue working with our law enforcement partners to target these schemes and hold those responsible accountable.”.

    Federal Communications Commission.

    Industry observers note that on Nov. 19, the FCC approved a latest rule to allow federal and state prisons and jails to use jamming technology to block calls from illegal contraband cell phones that can be used to coordinate outside illegal activity, including the jury duty scams described above as well as scams explicitly targeting U.S. veterans. The FCC has also taken concrete actions to target scammers and illegal robocallers. The FCC has stopped nearly 300 million illegal robocalls, saving Americans at least $38 million through enforcement and reforms that led to the blocking of more than 1,400 providers and 296 million illegal robocalls. This includes removing from networks voice providers who unlawfully transmitted illegal scammer calls impersonating government agencies, internet service providers, banks, and major retailers. The FCC has published step-by-step guides that enable consumers to turn on blocking and filtering tools specific to devices and carriers.

    “President Trump has put restoring law and order and ensuring the safety of law-abiding Americans at the top of his agenda and that includes stopping scammers. For years, hundreds of thousands of contraband cellphones have entered our prisons allowing offenders to perpetrate scams on ordinary Americans including veteran Jared Johns who took his life after inmates extorted and threatened him. By allowing jamming in prisons for the first time, we’re taking an aggressive, but responsible approach to eliminate inmates access to contraband phones," stated Chairman Carr. “The FCC continues to increase our work to crack down on scammers and protect consumers. We’ve taken extensive measures to strengthen consumers’ ability to revoke consent and stop unwanted calls including empowering consumers with instructions to block scam calls and texts, cutting off voices service providers from our networks after non-compliance and further incentivizing providers to block illegal calls so they never get to your phone in the first place.”.

    In a recent development, an indictment is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.
